summary.en: The Great Pyramid at Giza is built over about 26 years. It is completed around 2600 BC, according to datings of the mortar between 2620 and 2484 BC.

summary.en: On Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean, the last woolly mammoths live on until around 2000 BC, several centuries after the Pyramid of Cheops was built.

text.en: The sources only give when the last mammoths died, around 2000 BC (4,000 years ago). By then the mammoths had lived isolated on the island for about 6,000 years. The start year 2999 BC is not a figure from the sources but a lower limit for display, so that the event appears during the time of the pyramids.

summary.en: According to tradition, the first Olympic Games are held in 776 BC at Olympia, in honour of Zeus. The last known Games are held in AD 393.

summary.en: From 499 to 449 BC, Greek city-states fight the Persian Achaemenid Empire. The war begins with a revolt in the Greek cities of Asia Minor. The Persian kings Darius I and Xerxes I then attack Greece twice but are repelled at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea.

text.en: All surviving contemporary sources for the war are Greek, and no Persian account survives. The most important source is Herodotus, who wrote about the war around 440–430 BC. The end year 449 BC is tied to the disputed Peace of Callias.

intro.en: The Persian king Cyrus the Great conquered Ionia, the Greek cities in western Asia Minor, in 547 BC. The Persians ruled the cities through Greek tyrants, which led to discontent. In 499 BC Aristagoras, tyrant of Miletus, failed in a campaign against Naxos that he had undertaken with Persian support. He expected to be deposed and instead got the Ionian cities to revolt. Athens and Eretria sent help, and the rebels burned Sardis in 498 BC. Darius I swore to punish Athens and Eretria, and after the revolt he also wanted to stop the Greeks on the mainland from interfering in Asia Minor.

members.en: Mainly Athens and Sparta, with Corinth, Plataea, Thespiae and other cities, later the Delian League under Athens. In the revolt of 499–493 BC the Ionian cities, and later also rebellious Egyptians. Known commanders include Miltiades, Leonidas, Themistocles, Pausanias and Cimon.

The kings Darius I, Xerxes I and Artaxerxes I, with generals such as Datis, Artaphernes and Mardonius and Queen Artemisia I of Caria. Greek vassal states such as Thessaly, Boeotia, Thebes and Macedon also fought with the Persians.

outcome.en: The Greeks won. The Persian army left the Greek territories in Europe and Ionia, and Athens became the leading power through the Delian League. Athens in turn had to withdraw from Egypt and Cyprus. The war ended quietly after a Greek campaign to Cyprus in 451 BC. According to some ancient writers a peace, the Peace of Callias, was concluded, but this has been disputed since antiquity.

casualties.en: There is no overall estimate. Almost all figures come from Greek authors, mainly Herodotus, and modern historians consider them often too high. Herodotus wrote that Xerxes' army numbered 2.5 million men; today's scholars usually reckon with about 200,000. For Plataea, Herodotus gives 257,000 Persians dead, while modern estimates are 50,000–90,000.

summary.en: In 499 BC Greek cities in Asia Minor revolt against the Persians, led by Aristagoras of Miletus. With help from Athens and Eretria they burn the Persian provincial capital Sardis in 498 BC. The Persians then strike back, and the revolt is crushed in 493 BC.

In 494 BC the Persian fleet defeats the fleet of the Ionian cities at the island of Lade off Miletus. According to Herodotus the Ionians had 353 ships and the Persians 600. The victory nearly ends the revolt, and the Persians capture Miletus.

In 490 BC a Persian force under Datis and Artaphernes lands at Marathon. The Athenians and their allies from Plataea, 10,000–11,000 men under Miltiades among others, defeat the larger Persian army. The Persians' first attempt to conquer Greece is over.

text.en: The usual date is 12 September 490 BC, which August Böckh calculated in 1855 from Herodotus' information. If the Spartan calendar was a month ahead of Athens', it becomes 12 August instead. Wikidata gives both. According to Herodotus 6,400 Persians and 192 Athenians died; other estimates of the Persian losses are 1,000–2,000.

summary.en: In 480 BC about 7,000 Greeks under the Spartan king Leonidas block the pass at Thermopylae against Xerxes' army. They hold out for two days, until a local man shows the Persians a way around the pass. The Greek rearguard, with 300 Spartans, is wiped out, and the Persians can take Athens.

text.en: The year 480 BC is certain, but not the day. Wikipedia gives 21–23 July, 20 August or 8–10 September, and Wikidata gives July and 11 August. Ancient writers wrote that the Persian army was millions strong; modern scholars estimate it at 120,000–300,000.

summary.en: In September 480 BC the Athenian Themistocles lures the larger Persian fleet into the narrow strait at Salamis. There the Persians cannot make use of their greater numbers, and the Greeks win. It was perhaps the largest naval battle of antiquity, and it turned the war. Xerxes withdraws to Asia with a large part of the army.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 26 or 27 September 480 BC, and Wikidata gives 27 and 29 September. According to the source the Greeks lost 40 ships and the Persians 300.

caption.en: The Battle of Salamis as Wilhelm von Kaulbach painted it in the 19th century. Photograph of a full-size print of the painting, which is in the Bavarian Landtag. An artist's picture more than 2,000 years later, not a depiction from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: In August 479 BC a Greek army under Spartan leadership defeats the Persian army that Xerxes left behind under Mardonius. Mardonius is killed, and a large part of the Persian army is trapped in its camp and killed. Together with the naval battle at Mycale, this ends the Persians' second invasion.

text.en: The ancient figures differ greatly. For the Greek losses, Herodotus names 91 Spartans, 16 Tegeans and 52 Athenians killed (159 in all) and, in addition, 600 Megarians and Phliasians killed by Theban cavalry; Plutarch gives 1,360 and Diodorus 10,000. For the Persians, Wikipedia gives 257,000 dead according to Herodotus and 100,000 according to Diodorus. Modern scholars estimate the Persian army at 70,000–120,000 men and the Persian losses at 50,000–90,000. The source itself disagrees about Herodotus's Greek figure: its infobox says 159 and its main text 652. The date is given as 27 or 28 August.

summary.en: The Delian League under the Athenian Cimon defeats a Persian fleet and then a Persian army at the River Eurymedon in Asia Minor. After the double victory the Persians avoid major battles with the Greeks.

text.en: The sources do not agree on the year: most scholars place the battle in either 469 or 466 BC. Wikidata gives no year. For that reason the battle has only one checked source for the time.

summary.en: Around 449 BC Athens and Persia are said to have concluded peace through the Athenian Callias. If the peace existed, it gave the cities of Ionia self-government and closed the Aegean Sea to Persian warships, while Athens promised to leave Persian territories in peace. The war comes to an end around then in any case.

text.en: Even ancient writers disagreed about the peace. Diodorus writes that it was concluded, while Thucydides mentions no peace and Callisthenes and Theopompus seem to deny it. Among modern historians some accept the peace, while others believe there was only an agreement without a treaty. Wikidata gives 449 BC.

summary.en: From 336 to 323 BC the Macedonian king Alexander the Great conquers the Persian Achaemenid Empire. His army marches through Asia Minor, Syria, Egypt, Mesopotamia and Iran all the way to the River Indus in present-day Pakistan. When Alexander dies in Babylon in 323 BC, the empire is divided among his generals.

text.en: The war is counted here from 336 BC, when Alexander became king and began to put down the revolts in Greece, as in Wikipedia and Wikidata. The campaign against Persia itself began in 334 BC.

intro.en: In 336 BC Philip II of Macedon was murdered. He had gathered the Greek city-states under Macedonian leadership in the League of Corinth to wage war on Persia. His son Alexander was proclaimed king and became leader of the League. The news of Philip's death made Thebes, Athens, Thessaly and Thracian tribes revolt. Alexander put down the revolts and then marched east to carry out the plan to conquer the Achaemenid Empire.

members.en: Alexander the Great and his generals, among them Parmenion, with Macedonian troops and soldiers from the League of Corinth. Later also Phoenician cities such as Byblos and Sidon, and in India King Omphis of Taxila.

Mainly the Persian Achaemenid Empire under Darius III and his satraps, among them the Greek mercenary commander Memnon of Rhodes. In addition rebellious Greek cities such as Thebes, the city of Tyre, and in India King Porus of the Pauravas and mountain peoples such as the Aspasioi and Assakenoi.

outcome.en: Alexander won all the major battles. The Achaemenid Empire fell, and Darius III was killed during his flight east by Bessus, who led the Bactrian cavalry in his retinue. Alexander's empire stretched from the Balkans and Egypt to Central Asia and India. In India the soldiers refused to go further than the River Hyphasis (today the Beas) in 326 BC, and the army turned home, partly through the Gedrosian Desert. Alexander created no stable empire. After his death in 323 BC his generals, the Diadochi, fought for about 40 years over dividing it among themselves.

casualties.en: There is no reliable figure. Wikipedia gives more than a million dead and refers to the ancient writer Arrian. The figures for individual battles come from ancient writers and often differ greatly: at Gaugamela Curtius Rufus gives 40,000 and Diodorus 90,000 dead on the Persian side. According to Plutarch Alexander lost three quarters of his army in the Gedrosian Desert.

summary.en: In 335 BC the city of Thebes revolts against the Macedonians. Alexander takes the city and punishes it harshly: according to the source 6,000 were killed and 30,000 were sold as slaves, and the city was burned down except for the temples. The destruction shakes all of Greece, and other revolts die out before they have begun.

In May 334 BC, the same year he crossed the Hellespont to Asia, Alexander defeats the army of the Persian satraps at the River Granicus. It is the first of three major battles between Alexander and Persia. After the battle the Persians can only defend the cities they still hold in Asia Minor.

On 5 November 333 BC Alexander meets the Persian king Darius III for the first time. The Persian army is much larger, according to modern estimates 108,000–158,000 men against about 37,000, but Alexander wins. Darius flees and leaves behind his family and his treasury.

From January to July 332 BC Alexander besieges the Phoenician city of Tyre, which lay on an island one kilometre from the coast. He has a causeway built out to the island and finally breaks through the walls. According to Arrian 8,000 inhabitants were killed after the conquest, and 30,000 were sold as slaves.

On 1 October 331 BC Alexander and Darius III meet for the second and last time. The Macedonians are far fewer but win with better tactics. The battle is regarded as the decisive battle against the Achaemenid Empire, and Alexander then takes Babylon and Susa.

title.en: About the place and the figures

text.en: The battlefield was probably at Tel Gomel, but this is not entirely certain. The ancient figures for Persian dead differ: 40,000 according to Curtius Rufus and 90,000 according to Diodorus. Wikidata gives the same day and roughly the same place.

caption.en: The Battle of Arbela (Gaugamela) in Charles Le Brun's painting from 1669, photographed in the Louvre. An artist's picture nearly 2,000 years later, not a depiction from the time of the event. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In May 326 BC Alexander crosses the monsoon-swollen River Hydaspes and defeats King Porus of the Pauravas and his war elephants. Alexander lets Porus continue to rule as satrap. Further east, at the River Hyphasis, the soldiers refuse to go on, and Alexander turns back.

According to a Babylonian astronomical diary, Alexander dies in Babylon between the evening of 10 June and the evening of 11 June 323 BC, aged 32. He had planned a campaign to the Arabian Peninsula. His generals abandon the plans and begin to fight over the empire.

text.en: Why Alexander died has been debated for millennia, and historians interpret the ancient sources differently. The date is given in the Julian calendar. Wikidata gives the same day, 10 June 323 BC, but no place, so the place has only one checked source.

summary.en: Three wars between the Roman Republic and Carthage, with its capital in present-day Tunisia, from 264 to 146 BC. They are fought in Sicily, Italy, the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa. The Romans win all three, and the last ends with the destruction of Carthage.

text.en: Almost everything we know comes from Greek and Roman writers, not from Carthage. The most reliable source is considered to be Polybius, who was himself present at the fall of Carthage but wrote from a pro-Roman perspective. The Roman Livy is openly pro-Roman, and his accounts of battles are often inaccurate.

intro.en: The Roman Republic had conquered all of Italy south of the River Arno around 270 BC. Carthage, with its capital in present-day Tunisia, had a seafaring empire with the southern Iberian Peninsula, large parts of the North African coast, Corsica, Sardinia and western Sicily. The two states had long been friends and trading partners, but as they came closer to each other the risk of conflict grew. According to the source, they stumbled into war more by chance than by intent. The war began in 264 BC when the Romans entered Sicily at Messana.

members.en: The Roman Republic with allies in Italy, with commanders such as Gaius Duilius, Gaius Lutatius Catulus, Scipio Africanus and Scipio Aemilianus. In the second war also the Numidian ruler Masinissa.
Carthage with allies and mercenaries, among them Gauls, Iberians and Numidians, with commanders such as Hanno, Hannibal and his brothers Hasdrubal and Mago.

outcome.en: Rome won all three wars. After the first war (264–241 BC) Sicily became Rome's first province, and Carthage had to pay large indemnities. After the second (218–201 BC) Carthage lost its territories outside Africa, was allowed only a small army and was not allowed to make war without Rome's permission. In the third war (149–146 BC) the city of Carthage was destroyed, and its land became the Roman province of Africa. Rome thereby became the leading power in the western Mediterranean.

casualties.en: The sources give no overall figure for all three wars. The figures for individual battles come from ancient writers, mainly the Greek Polybius and the Roman Livy, and differ. At Cannae, according to Polybius, 70,000 Romans and allies were killed, according to Livy 48,200. When Carthage fell in 146 BC, 50,000 inhabitants were sold as slaves.

summary.en: In 260 BC Rome wins its first victory at sea, under Gaius Duilius against the Carthaginian Hannibal Gisco. The Romans use the corvus for the first time, a plank that fastens their ships to the enemy's so that the soldiers can cross over and take the ship.

On 10 March 241 BC the Roman fleet defeats a larger but poorly manned Carthaginian fleet that is heavily loaded with supplies. This decides the First Punic War after 23 years. Carthage makes peace, hands Sicily over to Rome and pays large indemnities.

In 219 BC Hannibal besieges the city of Saguntum on the Iberian Peninsula for eight months and captures it. Almost all of the city's defenders are killed. The siege becomes the direct cause of the Second Punic War.

In 218 BC Hannibal leads his army from the Iberian Peninsula over the Alps into Italy. In this way he avoids the Roman garrisons and Rome's fleet. It is regarded as one of the most famous military feats of antiquity.

text.en: No one knows for certain which route Hannibal took. The main sources, Polybius and Livy, wrote long afterwards, and there are no archaeological traces. The point on the map is Wikidata's and shows only roughly where in the Alps it was.

summary.en: On 2 August 216 BC Hannibal surrounds a much larger Roman army of about 86,000 men and destroys almost all of it. It is one of Rome's worst defeats and is regarded as one of the most skilful battles in military history. Afterwards Capua and several other Italian cities go over to Carthage.

text.en: The ancient writers give different losses: according to Polybius 70,000 Romans and allies were killed, according to Livy 48,200. On the Carthaginian side Polybius gives 5,700 dead and Livy 8,000.

summary.en: In 202 BC the Roman Scipio Africanus defeats Hannibal at Zama in North Africa. Carthage had 80 war elephants, but the Romans were stronger in cavalry. The defeat is so severe that Carthage gives up, and Hannibal is eventually forced into exile. The peace the following year ends Carthage as a great power.

text.en: Wikipedia gives only the year 202 BC. Wikidata gives 19 October 202 BC in the Julian calendar.

caption.en: The Battle of Zama in a picture by Cornelis Cort from 1567, in the Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery in Glasgow. An artist's picture more than 1,700 years later, not a depiction from the time of the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: After nearly three years of siege, the Romans under Scipio Aemilianus storm Carthage early in 146 BC. Over a week the city is destroyed and many inhabitants are killed, and 50,000 who are taken prisoner are sold as slaves. Carthage's land becomes the Roman province of Africa.

A civil war in China between the fall of the Qin dynasty in 206 BC and the founding of the Han dynasty in 202 BC. It is fought mainly between Xiang Yu, ruler of Western Chu, and Liu Bang, King of Han. Liu Bang wins and becomes the first emperor of the Han dynasty.

intro.en: After the death of Qin Shi Huang in 210 BC, major revolts broke out against the Qin dynasty. The rebel leader Liu Bang captured the capital Xianyang, and Qin's last ruler surrendered. The most powerful rebel leader, Xiang Yu of Chu, then divided the realm into eighteen kingdoms. Many rebels became discontented, because they received little or no land. Liu Bang was forced to make do with the remote Bashu and Hanzhong, although he had been promised Guanzhong, which instead went to three Qin generals who had surrendered. Soon new wars broke out, with revolts in Qi and Liu Bang's attack on Guanzhong.

members.en: Liu Bang, King of Han, with the general Han Xin, the adviser Zhang Liang and allies such as Ying Bu, Peng Yue and Zhang Er.

Xiang Yu, who called himself hegemon, with generals such as Long Ju, Zhongli Mo and Cao Jiu. For a time Western Wei and the three Qin kings also sided with Chu. Qi and Zhao fought against both at times.

outcome.en: Liu Bang won. Xiang Yu took his own life after the defeat at Gaixia, and the rest of Chu's forces surrendered. In February 202 BC Liu Bang ascended the throne as Emperor Gaozu and founded the Han dynasty. The capital became first Luoyang and then Chang'an. Liu Bang first rewarded his generals but later had most of the kings he had appointed removed or killed, among them Han Xin and Peng Yue.

casualties.en: The source gives no overall figure. For individual battles very large numbers are given: at Pengcheng Han is said to have lost over 200,000 men, and at Gaixia 80,000 of Xiang Yu's soldiers are said to have been killed and 20,000 taken prisoner. The source does not state where the figures come from, and such large ancient figures are uncertain.

summary.en: In 205 BC, while Xiang Yu is fighting in Qi, Liu Bang captures Chu's capital Pengcheng with a large army. Xiang Yu hurries back with 30,000 picked soldiers, attacks at dawn and defeats the unprepared Han army. Several members of Liu Bang's family are taken prisoner, and some of his allies go over to Chu.

text.en: The year 205 BC agrees in all sources, including Wikidata. Wikipedia's article on the battle gives April, while the article on the war says that Pengcheng fell to Liu Bang in September–October. The information that Liu Bang's army was 560,000 men comes from the same sources.

summary.en: In October 205 BC Han Xin meets a much larger army from Zhao in the Jingxing Pass. He pretends to flee and lures out Zhao's soldiers, while 2,000 horsemen take their weakly defended camp and raise Han's flags. Zhao's army dissolves in confusion, and Han Xin wins.

text.en: Wikidata gives the year 205 BC and the Jingxing Pass as the place, but no coordinates. The point on the map is the pass's location according to Wikipedia.

summary.en: In November 204 BC Han Xin defeats a combined army from Chu and Qi, with, according to the source, 200,000 Chu soldiers under Long Ju. Long Ju is killed and Qi's king Tian Guang is taken prisoner. Han Xin conquers all of Qi, and Chu's soldiers lose heart.

text.en: Wikidata gives the year 204 BC and the city of Weifang as the place, but no coordinates of its own for the battle. The point is Weifang's location and shows only roughly where it was.

summary.en: Liu Bang, Han Xin and Peng Yue surround Xiang Yu at Gaixia. Han Xin has his soldiers sing songs from Chu, so that Xiang Yu's men think their homeland has surrendered, and many desert. Xiang Yu breaks out with a small band but takes his own life at the Wujiang River. It was the last major battle of the war.

text.en: Wikipedia's articles on the battle and on the war give December 203 BC. The article on Liu Bang and Wikidata give 202 BC. For that reason both years are shown. The place is not entirely certain: the article on the battle gives today's Guzhen, the article on the war south-east of Lingbi.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of Chinese ink painting on a silk scroll, not a historical image.

summary.en: After the last resistance has been crushed, Liu Bang ascends the throne in February 202 BC. He is called Emperor Gaozu, and the dynasty is named Han. The capital becomes first Luoyang and is soon moved to Chang'an.

text.en: According to Liu Bang's biography in the Hanshu, he was crowned on the jiawu day of the second month, which Wikipedia and Wikidata (in the entry on Liu Bang's office) convert to 28 February 202 BC. The event has no entry of its own in Wikidata, and the place could not be compared.

summary.en: The philosopher Confucius is born around 551 BC in the state of Lu and dies around 479 BC. His teaching shapes China for over two thousand years.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of Chinese ink painting on silk, not a historical image.

summary.en: Between 230 and 221 BC the state of Qin conquers the six other warring states, one at a time. Qin's king Ying Zheng then proclaims himself China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang.

text.en: The years ultimately rest on ancient chronicles such as Sima Qian's Shiji and the Zhan Guo Ce. They give years but no dates, and several statements in Wikipedia's article are marked as insufficiently supported. Wikidata gives the same years, 230–221 BC, but Japan as the country, which is not correct. For that reason the war has only one checked source.

intro.en: In the Warring States period China was divided among seven states, and the kings of the Zhou dynasty had only a ceremonial role left. After Shang Yang's reforms in the 4th century BC, Qin became the strongest state. Ying Zheng took power in Qin in 238 BC and made a plan with Li Si among others: to stay on good terms with the distant states and attack the nearest ones, and to conquer the states one at a time.

members.en: The state of Qin under King Ying Zheng, with generals such as Wang Jian, Wang Ben, Li Xin and Meng Wu.
Han, Zhao (and its successor Dai), Yan, Wei, Chu and Qi. They fought separately and fell one after another.

outcome.en: Qi surrendered without a fight in 221 BC, and all of China was united under the Qin dynasty. Ying Zheng took the title Shi Huangdi, First Emperor. The old system of vassal states (fengjian) was replaced by a centrally ruled state with 36 commanderies and the capital Xianyang. The dynasty lasted only 15 years, but the Han dynasty, which took over, built on much of what Qin had created.

casualties.en: There is no overall estimate of how many died. The chronicles mention individual figures, for example that over 100,000 people, civilians included, died when Qin flooded Wei's capital Daliang in 225 BC. Ancient figures are uncertain, and several of the war's figures are marked as unsupported in the source.

summary.en: Qin's army crosses the Yellow River and captures Han's capital Zheng in 230 BC. King An of Han surrenders, and Han, the weakest of the states, becomes the first to fall.

Zhao's king has had his best general Li Mu executed, after Qin bribed a minister to accuse him of treason. In 228 BC Qin captures the capital Handan and takes King Qian prisoner. A brother of the king holds out in the state of Dai until 222 BC.

Yan's crown prince Dan has sent an assassin against Ying Zheng, but the assassination attempt fails. Qin attacks Yan in 226 BC and captures the capital Ji. Yan's king flees to the Liaodong Peninsula, where the last forces are defeated in 222 BC.

Qin's general Wang Ben besieges Wei's capital Daliang in 225 BC and for three months diverts water from the Yellow River and a canal until the city is flooded. Over 100,000 people die, civilians included, and King Jia of Wei surrenders.

A first Qin army under Li Xin is beaten back by Chu. Ying Zheng then sends a much larger army under Wang Jian (the figure given is 600,000 men), which defeats Chu's army and in 223 BC captures the capital Shouchun and takes King Fuchu prisoner.

Qin's army takes a detour through the conquered Yan and suddenly stands outside Qi's capital Linzi. King Tian Jian surrenders without a fight in 221 BC. Ying Zheng proclaims himself Shi Huangdi, China's first emperor.

summary.en: The philosopher Socrates is born around 470 BC in Athens and is sentenced to death in 399 BC.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of ancient Greek red-figure vase painting, not a historical image.

summary.en: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquers the kingdom of Kalinga on the Bay of Bengal, around 261 BC. According to Ashoka's own inscriptions 100,000 people were killed and 150,000 deported. The war made him renounce wars of conquest.

text.en: The year rests on Ashoka's own statement that he conquered Kalinga eight years after his coronation. The coronation is given as 268 BC or around 269 BC, and the war is therefore dated to around 261 BC. Wikidata and Wikipedia's article on the Rock Edict give 262–261 BC. The year is thus approximate.

intro.en: Kalinga was an independent and prosperous kingdom on the Bay of Bengal, in present-day Odisha and northern Andhra Pradesh, with ports and sea trade as far as Southeast Asia. It had been subject to the Nanda Empire until 321 BC, and Ashoka's grandfather Chandragupta may have tried to conquer it without succeeding. Ashoka marched against Kalinga as soon as he had secured his throne. Some scholars hold that Kalinga was a strategic threat to the Mauryan Empire, since it could cut the links between the capital Pataliputra and the empire's territories on the central peninsula, and since it controlled the coast and the trade on the Bay of Bengal.

members.en: The kingdom of Kalinga. The name of its ruler is unknown. According to the Greek Megasthenes, who stayed at Chandragupta's court, Kalinga's rulers had a strong army of infantry, cavalry and elephants.

outcome.en: Kalinga became part of the Mauryan Empire. In his thirteenth Major Rock Edict Ashoka writes that he deeply regrets the conquest. He then devoted the rest of his life to non-violence (ahimsa) and to winning through dharma instead of with weapons. The empire was not expanded further by war, and more than 40 years of relative peace followed. According to the sources Ashoka was already a Buddhist before the war. In Kalinga itself, at Dhauli and Jaugada, Rock Edicts 11–13 were not inscribed. There two separate edicts to the officials in the conquered land stand instead.

casualties.en: According to Ashoka's thirteenth Rock Edict 100,000 people were killed and 150,000 deported, and many more died of other causes. Wikipedia states that the war cost nearly 250,000 lives. The figures come from Ashoka himself, and the size of the armies is unknown.

summary.en: The Mauryan army defeats Kalinga, probably around 261 BC. The decisive battle is believed to have been fought at the hill of Dhauli by the River Daya. The war is regarded as one of the largest and bloodiest in India's history.

text.en: The sources state that the battle is believed to have been fought at Dhauli, so the place is not certain. On the hill today stand Ashoka's rock inscriptions and a peace pagoda from 1972. The event has no entry of its own in Wikidata and could not be compared with a second, independent source.

summary.en: Cleopatra, Egypt's last Ptolemaic ruler, is born in 70/69 BC in Alexandria and dies there in August 30 BC.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of ancient Roman fresco painting, not a historical image.

summary.en: Egypt under Ramesses II and the Hittite Empire fought over power in Syria. The war began when Ramesses took Amurru, continued with the Battle of Kadesh and ended around 1259 BC with the oldest surviving peace treaty. The years follow the usual so-called low chronology.

text.en: Egypt's dates from this time are uncertain. The sources follow the low chronology, in which the Battle of Kadesh was dated to May 1274 BC. With the high chronology all dates become about 20 years earlier. The war has no entry of its own in Wikidata, so the span rests on Wikipedia's articles on the battle and the treaty.

intro.en: Egypt and the Hittites had for over two hundred years fought over the lands of the eastern Mediterranean. Ramesses II's father Seti I had taken Kadesh and Amurru, but the areas then fell under the Hittites again. In his fourth regnal year Ramesses marched north and took the Hittite vassal state Amurru. The Hittite king Muwatalli II wanted to retake Amurru and moved south to meet the Egyptians, and the following year the armies met at Kadesh.

members.en: Egypt's New Kingdom under Pharaoh Ramesses II, with four army divisions (Amun, Ra, Set and Ptah), a troop called the ne'arin and mercenaries from the Sherden people.
The Hittite Empire under King Muwatalli II, later Hattusili III, with vassal kings and allies, among them the king of Aleppo. Ramesses listed 19 of the Hittites' allies at Kadesh.

outcome.en: Neither side won decisively. The Battle of Kadesh ended in a draw according to today's historians, although both sides said they had won. The Hittites kept Amurru and Kadesh, and Egypt's influence was limited to Canaan. Ramesses later took Dapur and Tunip but could not keep them. About 15 years after Kadesh, Ramesses II and Hattusili III concluded a peace treaty. It is the oldest known surviving peace treaty, and a copy hangs at the UN headquarters.

casualties.en: How many died is unknown. The sources give the losses at Kadesh as unknown, but write that both sides suffered heavy losses.

summary.en: In May 1274 BC Ramesses II meets the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh. The Egyptians were lured into an ambush but managed to turn the battle around. It is the oldest battle for which tactics and formations are known in detail, and probably the largest chariot battle ever fought, with 5,000–6,000 chariots. The outcome is regarded as a draw.

text.en: Egyptian inscriptions give the day as year 5, third month of shemu, day 9 of Ramesses II's reign. With the usual low chronology this becomes May 1274 BC, and with the high chronology about 20 years earlier. Almost all sources for the battle are Egyptian, and Ramesses' version is considered exaggerated; the Hittite texts instead describe Ramesses as having to withdraw.

caption.en: The city of Kadesh surrounded by the river Orontes, as shown in a relief from the time of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel. Drawing from the work of James Henry Breasted. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Ramesses II takes the fortified city of Dapur, which the inscriptions say lay in the land of the Hittites. The siege is depicted on the walls of his mortuary temple, the Ramesseum, with ladders, chariots and six of his sons. Within a year the area was again under Hittite control.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the siege gives 1269 BC, and the article on Ramesses II says his eighth and ninth regnal years. Wikidata gives 1271 BC. Where Dapur lay is also disputed: the city has often been identified with Tabor in Canaan, but the Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen argues that it lay in Syria north of Kadesh. The point on the map is Wikidata's and is approximate.

summary.en: Around 1259 BC Ramesses II and Hattusili III make peace, probably through envoys without the kings meeting. It is the oldest known surviving peace treaty, and the only one from the ancient Near East where both parties' versions survive: the Egyptian one in temple inscriptions at Thebes and the Hittite one on clay tablets from Hattusa.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the treaty was concluded around 1259 BC and ratified in Ramesses II's 21st regnal year, 1258 BC. Wikidata gives 1259 BC. The treaty is sometimes called the Treaty of Kadesh, but the battle is not mentioned in the text.

summary.en: Around 605 BC Babylonia and Egypt, with the remnants of the Assyrian army on the Egyptian side, meet at the trading and crossing city of Carchemish on the Euphrates. Crown Prince Nebuchadnezzar II leads the Babylonians and Pharaoh Necho II the Egyptians. Babylonia wins decisively, Egypt's influence in the Levant comes to an end and Babylon expands all the way to the Egyptian border.

In 38 BC a Parthian army under Prince Pacorus, son of King Orodes II, again enters Syria. The Roman general Publius Ventidius Bassus meets it with his legions on the heights at Gindarus and wins a decisive victory. Pacorus is killed, and the Parthian invasions of Syria are halted.

text.en: The battle has no entry of its own in Wikidata that could be found, so the year and place come from Wikipedia. The Historical Conflict Event Dataset gives the same year and almost the same place.

summary.en: The Senones, a Gallic people under Brennus who have entered northern Italy, defeat the army of the Roman Republic at the river Allia near Rome. The battle is usually dated to 390 BC according to tradition, but it probably took place in 387 BC.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 387 BC as the probable year and 390 BC as the traditional one. Wikidata has both years, and the Historical Conflict Event Dataset gives 390 BC. We show 387 BC with uncertainty.

summary.en: According to the Gospels, Jesus is born in Bethlehem in the time of King Herod. The year is not stated in any source from the time. Counting back from Herod's death, it falls between 6 and 4 BC.

text.en: Our calendar era counts from the year in which Jesus was once believed to have been born. The monk Dionysius Exiguus devised it in Rome in the year 525, but it only became common in the 9th century. There is no year 0: after 1 BC comes 1 AD directly. Today scholars believe that Jesus was born a few years earlier, perhaps around 5 BC. The sources are not enough for a certain year.

caption.en: The Nativity of Jesus as Giotto painted it in the 14th century: fresco in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, 1306 according to the file page. An artist's image made over a thousand years later, not a depiction from the time of the event. Detail. Public domain.

summary.en: The Buddha, a wandering teacher on the Gangetic plain, founds Buddhism. He lived in the 6th or 5th century BC, and scholars disagree on exact dates. According to tradition he attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.

caption.en: A small temple under the Bodhi Tree at Bodh Gaya, the place where the Buddha according to tradition attained enlightenment. Painting by an unknown artist, around 1810, over 2,000 years after the Buddha's time. Detail. Public domain.

summary.en: From around 10,000 to 8000 BC people in the Fertile Crescent in Southwest Asia begin to cultivate crops and keep domesticated animals. Among the plants domesticated here are einkorn wheat, emmer wheat, barley, lentils, peas, chickpeas and flax, as well as sheep, goats and pigs. The earliest known farming villages lie around the Jordan River and the upper Euphrates. Agriculture also arises independently elsewhere, including in China, the New Guinea highlands, Mexico, northern South America and Africa.

caption.en: The excavations at Jarmo in northern Iraq, one of the early farming villages in the Fertile Crescent, photographed in 2021. Modern photo. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: In the city of Uruk in Sumer are the oldest known examples of writing, from the end of the fourth millennium BC. Cuneiform, the oldest known writing system, grows out of pictographic signs and out of a system of clay tokens used in accounting. The signs are drawn and pressed into clay tablets with a sharp reed stylus. Cuneiform is used for more than 3,000 years: the last securely dated tablet, also from Uruk, dates from AD 79/80.

caption.en: Clay tablet with early writing from the Uruk III period, end of the fourth millennium BC, in the Louvre. Modern museum photo. Licence: CC BY 3.0.

summary.en: Around 3100 BC, with an uncertainty of about 150 years, the reign of King Narmer begins. Many scholars see him as the one who united Egypt and founded the first dynasty. The Narmer Palette, a carved stone slab, was found at Hierakonpolis in the 1897–1898 season.

text.en: The date of about 3100 BC (± 150 years) is based partly on the Turin Canon, an ancient list of kings. A 2013 study using radiocarbon dating places the reign of his successor Aha most likely in 3111–3045 BC. Other mainstream estimates fall within about 3173–2987 BC. Whether the First Dynasty began with Narmer or with Aha is also disputed.

caption.en: The Narmer Palette from Hierakonpolis. It shows King Narmer striking down an enemy. Modern photo from 2002. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: The city of Caral in the Supe Valley in Peru, 23 kilometres from the coast, was inhabited from around 2600 to 2000 BC. It is the capital of the Caral culture, which emerged between 3000 and 1800 BC, and one of the largest sites of the Norte Chico civilisation. Around 3,000 people lived there. Caral has been called the oldest city in the Americas, but finds at other ancient sites nearby have called that into question. The city became a World Heritage Site in 2009.

caption.en: The Great Pyramid and the circular plaza at Caral in Peru. Modern photo. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain in England is built in several stages from around 3100 to 1600 BC. The great ring of sarsen stones is raised between 2600 and 2400 BC. The smaller bluestones probably come from the Preseli Hills in southwest Wales. The monument is aligned with the sunrise at midsummer and the sunset at midwinter. It became a World Heritage Site in 1986.

caption.en: Stonehenge, photographed in 2007. Modern photo. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: Around 2500 BC Mohenjo-daro is built on the lower Indus. It becomes one of the largest cities of the Indus civilisation and one of the world's earliest large cities, with perhaps 40,000 inhabitants, although that figure is uncertain. The city has a great bath, covered drains along the main streets and over 700 wells. It is abandoned around 1700 BC and in 1980 became South Asia's first World Heritage Site.

caption.en: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, photographed in 2014. Modern photo. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Around 1753 BC Hammurabi, the sixth king of Babylon's first dynasty, has a collection of laws compiled. It is the longest and best organised law text from the ancient Near East, and the laws are numbered up to 282. One principle behind many of them is an eye for an eye. The main copy is inscribed on a basalt stele about 2.25 metres high, which was found at Susa in 1901 and is today in the Louvre.

caption.en: The stele with Hammurabi's laws in the Louvre. Modern museum photo. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: Around 1600 BC the volcanic island of Thera (Santorini) in the Aegean Sea has one of the largest volcanic eruptions in human history. The city of Akrotiri is buried under pumice and ash. On Crete, where the Minoan culture existed, tsunamis up to nine metres high wash over coastal settlements, and earthquakes destroy several sites.

text.en: The dating is disputed. Carbon-14 dates give various ranges between about 1680 and 1500 BC, while archaeological finds point to about 1550–1480 BC.

caption.en: At the Akrotiri excavation site on Santorini, the city that was buried by the eruption. Modern photo from 2012. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Around 1000 BC the Lapita people have reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, the furthest east of all the places where the Lapita culture is found. A find at Mulifanua on Samoa is about 3,000 years old. The Lapita people spread by sea across Melanesia from around 1600 BC and are known for their pottery with stamped patterns. They are direct ancestors of the peoples of Polynesia.

caption.en: Lapita pottery in the Vanuatu Cultural Centre in Port Vila. The vessels come from Vanuatu, not from Samoa. Modern museum photo. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In 510 BC the tyrant Hippias, son of Peisistratos, is overthrown in Athens with the help of Spartan soldiers. In 508/507 BC Cleisthenes carries out reforms that give power to the citizens. The four old tribes, which were based on kinship, are replaced by ten new ones based on where people live, divided into smaller units called demes. The Council is enlarged from 400 to 500 members, 50 from each tribe. The Assembly meets on the hill of the Pnyx. Cleisthenes is called the father of Athenian democracy.

caption.en: The Pnyx in Athens, where the Assembly met, with the Acropolis in the background. Modern photo from 2018. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: In 138 BC Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty sends the envoy Zhang Qian westwards. He is captured by the Xiongnu and held as a slave for thirteen years, but finally reaches the kingdom of Dayuan in the Fergana Valley and describes Bactria. In 125 BC he is back. His journey is regarded as the beginning of the trade route between East and West that later came to be called the Silk Road.

caption.en: Zhang Qian's journey westwards, mural in the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang from the 7th or 8th century. Later image. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 15 March 44 BC, the Ides of March, Julius Caesar is assassinated in the Curia of Pompey in Rome. About 60 senators take part, led by among others Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus, and Caesar receives about 23 stab wounds. The murder is followed by new civil wars, the Republic falls and the Roman Empire emerges under Augustus.

caption.en: The assassination of Julius Caesar, painting by Vincenzo Camuccini from 1804–1805. Later image. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On a mountain top in southeastern Turkey people built large circular structures with T-shaped stone pillars, around 9500–8000 BC. The pillars are regarded as the world's oldest known megaliths, and many are decorated with reliefs of wild animals. The site was built in the early Neolithic, before pottery existed. No one knows for certain what the structures were used for, but finds from 2019 suggest that people also lived there. Göbekli Tepe became a World Heritage Site in 2018.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the site was used until around 8000 BC, perhaps somewhat later. Wikidata states that it was abandoned during the 7000s BC (the millennium). The start year agrees in both sources (about 9500 BC, within the 10th millennium BC).

caption.en: Göbekli Tepe. Modern photo (2011). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: The Terracotta Army is thousands of figures of fired clay representing the army of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China. Work on his tomb complex began in 246 BC, and the figures were buried with the emperor in 210–209 BC to protect him after death. The three pits that have been investigated were estimated in 2007 to hold over 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots and hundreds of horses. Farmers digging a well found the army in 1974.

text.en: Wikipedia states that work on the tomb complex began in 246 BC and that the army was buried in 210–209 BC. Wikidata gives its creation as 248 BC, with a range from 246 to 208 BC.

caption.en: The Terracotta Army in Xi’an. Modern photo (2012). Detail. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: Teotihuacan was a large city about 40 kilometres northeast of present-day Mexico City. It was probably founded around 100 BC, and the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon were built here. At its height it was the largest city in the Americas, with probably around 100,000 inhabitants. Around AD 550 the city's great buildings were plundered and burned, but people continued to live there on a smaller scale. The Aztecs, who came much later, gave the city its name.

The Nok culture in central Nigeria is dated to roughly 1500 BC–1 BC. It is known for its terracotta sculptures, first found in 1928 near the village of Nok; the oldest may date from around 900 BC. Apart from Egyptian art, they are regarded as the oldest large three-dimensional figure sculptures in Africa. Iron smelting may have developed in the Nok culture between 750 and 550 BC.

King Piye of Kush, who ruled from Napata in present-day Sudan, invaded Egypt in his twentieth regnal year. He won at Herakleopolis, took Hermopolis after a five-month siege and conquered Memphis, and the kings of the Nile Delta submitted. The victory is described on a victory stele found at Gebel Barkal. Piye is regarded as the founder of Egypt's 25th dynasty but then returned to Nubia and never came back to Egypt.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on Piye gives the reign as 744–714 BC, while the article on the victory stele gives about 747–716 BC. Neither gives an exact year for the campaign, only regnal year 20, which becomes about 728–725 BC depending on which start one counts from. Wikidata states that Piye died in 716 BC.

summary.en: King Aspelta moved the capital of the Kingdom of Kush from Napata south to Meroë on the Nile, possibly around 591 BC, shortly after Pharaoh Psamtik II had plundered Napata. Meroë was the capital for several centuries, until the fall of the kingdom in the 4th century AD. From about 280 BC the kings were buried at Meroë instead of at Napata, and the site today has over 200 pyramids.

In her ninth regnal year, around 1471 BC, Pharaoh Hatshepsut sent a trading expedition of five ships to the land of Punt. According to the temple texts it was led by the chancellor Nehsi, and it returned with, among other things, 31 living myrrh trees and incense. The journey is depicted in reliefs in her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, and planks from the expedition have been found at the port of Mersa Gawasis on the Red Sea. Where Punt lay is debated, but most scholars place it in the Horn of Africa.

In the 5th century BC the Carthaginian Hanno led a fleet of 60 ships from Carthage, through the Strait of Gibraltar and south along Africa's Atlantic coast. Along the coast of present-day Morocco he founded or resettled seven colonies. How far he got is disputed: estimates range from southern Morocco to Gabon. His own account of the voyage survives only in abridged Greek copies.

Alexander the Great founded Alexandria on Egypt's Mediterranean coast in 331 BC, near the older Egyptian settlement of Rhakotis. He left Egypt a few months later and never returned to the city. In 305 BC Ptolemy I made Alexandria his capital, and within a century it had become the largest city in the world.

Around 240 BC Eratosthenes, who became chief librarian at Alexandria, calculated the circumference of the Earth. At noon on the summer solstice a stick cast no shadow at Syene (present-day Aswan), but there were shadows at Alexandria. The shadow angle, about 7.2 degrees or one fiftieth of a circle, and the distance of about 5,000 stadia between the cities gave an answer. Later authors give about 250,000 stadia, but both that figure and how long a stadion was are disputed.

Between about 1700 and 1100 BC the Indigenous people of present-day Louisiana built large earthworks at Poverty Point. The core is six C-shaped ridges in rings around a plaza, and the largest mound, Mound A, is 22 metres high. The site is regarded as the largest and most complex earthwork from the Late Archaic period in North America and became a World Heritage Site in 2014.

San Lorenzo in Veracruz was the most important centre of Olmec culture from around 1400 to 900 BC. The site is best known for the colossal stone heads; the largest weigh 28 tonnes or more and are about 3 metres high. The basalt was quarried in the Tuxtla Mountains and transported over 150 kilometres. Around 900 BC La Venta took over as the main centre, and why San Lorenzo fell is unknown.

Chavín de Huántar in Ancash was built in several stages from before 1200 BC and was the religious centre of the Chavín people, perhaps with an oracle. In the middle of the old temple stood the Lanzón, a figure with a feline head and a human body that is thought to have been the supreme god. The site was used for ceremonies until about 500 BC and is today a World Heritage Site.

Around 500 BC Monte Albán was founded on a levelled mountain ridge about 400 metres above the Oaxaca Valley. For almost a thousand years the city was the most important centre of the Zapotecs. Around 300 BC an estimated 5,200 people lived there, and from about 100 BC to AD 200 it was the capital of a state that dominated large parts of the Oaxaca highlands.

In the desert of southern Peru people made gigantic figures and lines in the ground by moving aside the reddish-brown stones so that lighter soil showed. Together the lines are over 1,300 kilometres long, and among the figures are a hummingbird, a condor, a monkey and a spider. They were probably created between about 500 BC and AD 500. What they were for is debated, but scholars most often think they had religious significance.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the lines were made between 500 BC and AD 500, in a Paracas phase (400–200 BC) and a Nazca phase (200 BC–AD 500). Wikidata gives 200 BC as the start.

caption.en: The Nazca Lines in Peru. Modern photo (2015). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: The Long Count was a Mesoamerican calendar that counted days and used zero as a placeholder. The oldest contemporary date found is on Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo and reads as 7.16.3.2.13, that is December 36 BC. The dating is not certain: the inscription can also be read as AD 182, and a stela at Takalik Abaj in Guatemala may be older.

text.en: Only the day name and the numbers 7.16.3.2.13 survive. Wikipedia gives both December 36 BC and October AD 182 as possible readings.

summary.en: El Mirador in northern Guatemala was a large Maya city of the Preclassic period. It flourished from roughly the 6th century BC to the 2nd century AD and was at its largest from the 3rd century BC. The city was linked to other cities by 13 raised causeways and has the pyramid of La Danta. Around AD 150 it was abandoned, like almost all the large sites in the area.

About 3,500 years ago the Lapita culture suddenly appears in the Bismarck Archipelago, fully developed and without traces of earlier stages. This suggests that it arrived with people who migrated in by sea. The classic Lapita pottery with stamped geometric patterns was made there between about 1600 and 1200 BC, and the finds at Talepakemalai on Mussau belong to the earliest group. The Lapita people are ancestors of the peoples of Polynesia, eastern Micronesia and the islands of Melanesia.

The Kerma culture, or the Kingdom of Kerma, had its centre in the city of Kerma in Nubia. It emerged from around 2500 BC and was at its largest between about 1750 and 1500 BC, when the city became a true city of about 25 hectares with large royal tombs and the temple building Western Deffufa. Between 1575 and 1550 BC Kerma pushed deep into Egypt. Under Thutmose I Egypt counterattacked, and around 1504 BC the area was annexed.

text.en: Wikipedia has the Kerma culture beginning around 2500 BC and mentions a preceding pre-Kerma culture from 3500 BC. Wikidata gives 3500 BC as the start year.

summary.en: D'mt was a kingdom in present-day Eritrea and northern Tigray in Ethiopia. The capital may have been at Yeha, where a large temple still stands. The culture is dated by carbon-14 to roughly 800/700–400 BC, but the exact years are unknown. Towards the end the large buildings at Yeha were abandoned, and later Aksum emerged in the same highlands.

text.en: The source says that the exact period of the kingdom is unknown. It mentions both roughly 800/700–400 BC (carbon-14) and the hypothesis of the late 8th century to the 6th century BC. Wikidata gives no year.

summary.en: Carthage was founded around 814 BC by merchants from Tyre, a Phoenician city-state in present-day Lebanon. According to legend, Queen Elissa, or Dido, was the founder of the city, but it is uncertain whether she existed. The city grew from a Phoenician colony into the capital of a kingdom that dominated the western Mediterranean.

Djenné-Djenno lies about 3 km from present-day Djenné and is counted among the oldest city-like sites in West Africa. Excavations, mainly by Roderick and Susan McIntosh, show that the site was inhabited from around 250 BC to around AD 1400. The site shows that long-distance trade and complex societies existed in West Africa before traders came from the north.

The Garamantes had settled in Fezzan by about 1000 BC at the latest and built a civilisation there that lasted until the end of the 7th century AD. Herodotus wrote about them in the 5th century BC. They dug tunnels, foggaras, to reach fossil groundwater beneath the desert, which made agriculture possible. The capital Garama lay at present-day Germa; when the groundwater sank, this may have contributed to the end of the kingdom.

The Paracas culture existed in the present-day Ica region of Peru from around 800 to around 100 BC. The people were skilled in irrigation and are known for their textiles. In the cemetery of Wari Kayan on the Paracas Peninsula the dead were wrapped in a seated position in many layers of finely woven and embroidered cloth, regarded as among the finest made in the pre-Columbian Andes. Paracas lacked a central ruler and consisted of local chiefdoms.

text.en: Wikipedia gives about 800–100 BC, while Wikidata gives 900–200 BC. The span is therefore given as approximate.

summary.en: The Adena culture was a group of related Native American societies with shared burial customs, from around 500 BC to around AD 100. It was centred in present-day Ohio but extended into neighbouring states. It is the best known of several cultures in eastern North America that began building ceremonial earthen mounds, and it is regarded as a predecessor of the Hopewell tradition. Through a far-reaching trade network they obtained, among other things, copper from the Great Lakes and seashells from the Gulf of Mexico. The name comes from a large mound near Chillicothe.

There are traces of early agriculture at Tikal as early as around 1000 BC. Large building projects with pyramids and platforms began around 400–300 BC, but the city was then smaller than El Mirador and Nakbe further north. During the first century AD rich tombs appeared and Tikal flourished while the large neighbours to the north declined. According to later inscriptions the royal dynasty was founded by Yax Ehb Xook, perhaps in the first century AD.

caption.en: The Great Plaza (Plaza Mayor) at Tikal. Modern photo (2007). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Kaminaljuyu in present-day Guatemala City was inhabited from around 1500 BC to AD 1200 and was the largest site in the southern Maya area. Its peak, the Miraflores period, is dated to around 400–100 BC, but a more recent dating moves it to around 100 BC–AD 100. Then large thrones and stelae were erected, and many monuments received early hieroglyphic texts. The city had advanced systems for managing water. Today most of the remains lie beneath the city.

Izapa in Chiapas was the largest site in the state and had its heyday between about 850 and 100 BC. The site is known for its sculpture: the researcher Garth Norman has counted 89 stelae, 61 altars and 3 thrones. The stelae often stand together with altars shaped like frogs, where the toads stood for rain. The images show myths and religious motifs and rarely have writing signs. The term Izapan style is used for similar works in other parts of the region.

The Ptolemaic kingdom built a lighthouse on the island of Pharos off Alexandria in the time of Ptolemy II; the construction years are given as between 284 and 246 BC. It was probably at least 100 metres high and one of the tallest structures in the world for many centuries. The lighthouse is counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Earthquakes damaged it badly between 956 and 1303, and in 1480 the last stones were used for Qaitbay's citadel.

caption.en: The Lighthouse of Pharos, a reconstruction drawing by the archaeologist Hermann Thiersch from 1909, not a contemporary image. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Dingoes must have come to Australia with people in boats, via the islands of Southeast Asia, but exactly when is uncertain. The oldest secure bones come from the Madura Caves on the Nullarbor Plain and have been dated directly by carbon-14 to between 3,348 and 3,081 years before present, that is around 1400–1130 BC. Dingoes are not found in Tasmania and thus arrived after the island had been separated from the mainland by the rising sea.

text.en: The article on the prehistory of Australia states that the dingo arrived about 4,000 years ago, roughly at the same time as the Pama–Nyungan languages spread across the mainland. The article on the dingo gives the bones from Madura as the oldest secure finds and writes that the dingo may have arrived later than previously thought.

summary.en: The Ambum Stone is a small stone sculpture from the New Guinea highlands that is believed to have been carved around 1500 BC. No one knows for certain which animal it represents; suggestions include an echidna, a flying fox, a bird or an extinct marsupial. Nor is its purpose known, but it may have been used as a pestle. It was found in a cave in the Ambum Valley and is today in the National Gallery of Australia.

text.en: The source mentions the Ambum Valley in Western Highlands Province but gives no coordinates. The point shows the province.

summary.en: Wandjina are cloud and rain spirits in the beliefs of the peoples of the Wanjina Wunggurr cultural area in the Kimberley, and they are a common motif in the rock art there. The broad-brushed Wandjina art is dated to about 3,800–4,000 years ago. The style arose when a drought that had lasted for about a thousand years ended and the climate became wetter, with regular monsoons.

At Teouma on the island of Efate lies the oldest known cemetery in the Pacific Islands, from the Lapita culture. In 2003, 36 buried people were found there. Some time after burial the heads of the dead had been removed and replaced with rings of cone shells, and in one grave three skulls lay on the chest of an older man. DNA from three of the women shows that they are genetically closest to people in Taiwan and the northern Philippines.

text.en: The article on Teouma states that the cemetery is about 3,200–3,000 years old but also speaks of the Lapita people in the 10th and 9th centuries BC. The article on the Lapita culture states that it was in use around 1000 BC. Wikidata gives the place but no time.

summary.en: Fiji was settled by the Austronesian Lapita people around 1100–1000 BC. On the island of Moturiki are some of Fiji's oldest Lapita settlements. There in 2002 the skeleton of a woman was found who was given the name Mana, “the truth”. She lived around 800 BC, and her skeleton is the best preserved from the Lapita period and the oldest found on Fiji. After examinations in Japan she was reburied on Moturiki in 2003.

text.en: The article on the history of Fiji gives 1100–1000 BC for the first settlement but 1500–1000 BC in its introduction, and settlements on Moturiki from 600 BC, perhaps 900 BC. The article on Moturiki states that the Naitabale settlement probably existed in 900 BC and that the skeleton dates from around 700 BC. The article on Mana gives 800 BC or earlier.

summary.en: Around the beginning of our calendar era many new inhabitants came to Fiji, mainly of Melanesian origin, about a thousand years after the Lapita people. Little is known about what happened to the first inhabitants, but they may have influenced the new culture. Fijian culture resembles the Melanesian culture of the western Pacific but has strong ties to the older Polynesian cultures, and how the peoples migrated is still not fully understood.

Vanuatu was settled about 3,000 years ago by Austronesian-speaking Lapita people, and the oldest pottery shards are from around 1300 BC. Around 500 BC a second wave of Melanesian peoples probably followed. Genetic studies show that immigration from Papuan groups in parts of Melanesia led to the population gradually being replaced.

Tonga was the first island group in Polynesia where the Lapita people settled. They came first to Tongatapu and shortly afterwards to Haʻapai. At the village of Nukuleka on Tongatapu a coral file has been dated by the uranium–thorium method to 888 BC, which gives an exact year for the earliest settlement there. The archaeologist David Burley has called Nukuleka the cradle of Polynesia, but that conclusion has been questioned.

text.en: The article on the history of Tonga also mentions a shell from Pea on Tongatapu dated to 3,180 ± 100 years before present, and elsewhere gives about 3,000 or 2,850 years before present (900 BC) for the arrival of the Lapita people. Wikidata gives the place but no time.

summary.en: Around 700 BC the Lapita people's decorated pottery in Tonga was replaced by simple, undecorated vessels, and from this time the inhabitants can be called Polynesians. They cultivated more, for example taro, yams, breadfruit and banana, and chickens became a larger part of the diet. The population grew, and villages spread onto Tongatapu. In the end people stopped making pottery altogether, and the same thing happened on Fiji and Samoa.

text.en: The article on the history of Tonga states that pottery ceased about 1,550 years before present, that is around the year 400. The article on the early history of Tonga gives the same time but converts it to 400 BC, and the article on Austronesian peoples gives about 400 BC. The article on the Lapita culture gives about 2,000 years ago.

summary.en: The island of Taumako in the Solomon Islands was settled by about 900 BC at the latest by the Lapita people. Archaeological investigations show that they made their pottery from clay and sand from the island. The Lapita culture had already spread to the Solomon Islands around 1200 BC, and from there it continued east towards Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.

The Lapita culture is named after a site on the Foué Peninsula on New Caledonia's main island, Grande Terre. There the American archaeologists Edward W. Gifford and Richard Shutler Jr. dug in 1952, and the settlement and the pottery shards were later dated to around 800 BC. The name comes from the archaeologists mishearing the word xapeta'a in the local language Haveke, which means roughly “dig a hole”. The oldest traces of people in New Caledonia are from the Lapita period.

text.en: The article on New Caledonia gives the oldest traces as around 1600–500 BC or 1300–200 BC. Gifford himself dated the finds to 2,800–2,450 years before present. The site's coordinates come from Wikidata.

summary.en: Nauru was settled by Micronesians about 3,000 years ago, and there are traces of possible Polynesian influence. The inhabitants lived on coconuts and pandanus fruit. They also caught young milkfish, accustomed them to fresh water and raised them in the Buada Lagoon. Traditionally there were twelve clans on the island, and today they are seen in the twelve-pointed star on Nauru's flag.

The people of the Torres Strait Islands settled the islands between Cape York and New Guinea about 4,000 years ago. In culture and language they differ from the Aboriginal peoples of the mainland. They were seafarers who lived by seasonal cultivation and by the resources of the reef and the sea. On some islands agriculture developed, and in the 14th century there were villages.

Ubirr is a rock formation in Kakadu National Park that is known for its Aboriginal rock paintings. The rock walls have been painted and repainted over a very long time, but most of the paintings were made about 2,000 years ago. Among them is so-called X-ray art and a painting of a thylacine, an animal that has been extinct in the area for about 2,000 years.

caption.en: Rock art at Ubirr in Kakadu National Park, Northern Territory. Modern photograph by Dietmar Rabich, 31 October 2019. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Independence I was a Paleo-Eskimo culture that lived in northern Greenland and the Canadian Arctic between about 2400 and 1900 BC. It is named after Independence Fjord in Peary Land. Together with the Saqqaq culture to the south, it is counted among the earliest known cultures in Greenland. The dwellings had a central passage and a hearth in the middle, to keep warm in the harsh landscape.

text.en: When the culture ended is debated. Wikipedia's article on the culture gives about 1900 BC, the article on the Saqqaq culture about 1300 BC, and Wikidata 1000 BC. The beginning, about 2400 BC, is the same in all three. Lex's overview of Greenland's prehistory gives about 2400–1800 BC.

summary.en: The Saqqaq culture is the earliest known archaeological culture in southern Greenland. It existed from about 2500 to about 800 BC and is named after the settlement of Saqqaq, where many finds have been made. No other culture has lived in Greenland for so long. It existed at the same time as the Independence I culture in northern Greenland.

text.en: Lex's overview of Greenland's prehistory gives about 2500–800 BC, as here. Lex's own article on the Saqqaq culture gives 2400–700 BC in its text.

summary.en: Around 2000 BC the Ortoiroid people began moving into the Antilles in the Caribbean. They were the second wave of people to settle there, after the Casimiroid peoples. They are thought to have come from the Orinoco valley in South America and moved from Trinidad and Tobago to Puerto Rico. The name comes from Ortoire, a shell midden in south-eastern Trinidad.

Around 1000 BC the Norton tradition developed along the Alaskan coast of the Bering Strait, and it lasted until about AD 800. The people used flaked stone tools like their predecessors but relied more on the sea and began to use oil lamps and clay pots. They hunted caribou, smaller mammals, salmon and large sea mammals and lived in villages they returned to after the hunting season.

text.en: The source is not consistent about the start: the lead gives about 1000 BC, which is used here, while the separate stages further down give Choris 1600–500 BC, Norton 500 BC–AD 800 and Ipiutak AD 1–800.

summary.en: Kuntur Wasi, “condor house” in Quechua, is the ruin of a religious centre on La Copa hill in the northern highlands of Peru, about 2,300 metres above sea level. It was first built around 1100–900 BC and was in use until about 50 BC. It has a hilltop temple, quadrangular platforms and a sunken courtyard. Its inhabitants are thought to have had a link with the Chavín culture.

At Paso de la Amada on the Gulf of Tehuantepec in Chiapas, archaeologists found in 1995 the remains of a ballcourt that has been dated to about 1400 BC. It is the oldest known ballcourt in Mesoamerica. It is about 80 metres long and 8 metres wide and lies between two parallel mounds with benches. The site was probably inhabited from about 1800 to 1000 BC.

The Dorset culture was a Paleo-Eskimo culture in the North American Arctic from about 500 BC. It followed the Pre-Dorset culture and preceded the Thule people, the ancestors of the Inuit. It is named after Cape Dorset, now Kinngait, where the first finds were made. Typical finds are triangular end blades and soapstone oil lamps. The Dorset appear to have disappeared by 1500 at the latest, perhaps as early as about 1000.

text.en: When the culture ended is uncertain: Wikipedia gives 1500 at the latest and perhaps as early as about 1000. Wikidata gives 500 BC–1500.

summary.en: The Paracas culture in present-day Peru shows the earliest evidence of trepanation in the Americas: with stone tools, sections of the skull were scraped and drilled away. A likely reason was to treat skull fractures, which are common among Paracas remains. The healing of the bone shows that nearly 40 percent of those operated on survived long-term, while 39 percent died during or shortly after the procedure.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the Paracas culture gives about 800–100 BC, which is used here. The article on trepanning gives 700 BC–AD 300 for the culture.

summary.en: Tak'alik Ab'aj in present-day Guatemala is one of several Mesoamerican sites with both Olmec and Maya features. The city flourished from the 9th century BC to at least the 10th century AD and was an important centre of commerce, trading with Kaminaljuyu and Chocolá among others. It lay where a river could be crossed, which was probably important when the city was founded, since trade routes were channelled through the site.

At the Maya site of San Bartolo in Petén, a team led by William Saturno found murals that have been carbon-dated to about 100 BC, the oldest Maya murals found so far. The paintings are still heavily influenced by Olmec tradition. The site also has the earliest inscriptions that are identifiably Maya, from the 3rd century BC.

The Lothagam North Pillar Site is a communal cemetery on the west side of Lake Turkana, built between 3000 and 2300 BC by the region's earliest herders, as rainfall decreased and the lake receded. It is thought to be eastern Africa's largest and earliest monumental cemetery. It is flanked by megaliths, stone circles and cairns and is believed to hold hundreds of people, many adorned with beads of stone, ivory, animal teeth and rings.

Around 2150 BC Egypt was hit by a series of exceptionally low Nile floods. They occurred during the global climate event known as the 4.2-kiloyear event. After a famine, they may have contributed to the collapse of the central government of the Old Kingdom.

text.en: Wikipedia writes that the low floods may have influenced the collapse of the Old Kingdom. The connection is a hypothesis, not established.

summary.en: Baqet III was governor of the Oryx nome in Upper Egypt during the 11th Dynasty, in the 21st century BC. His rock-cut tomb at Beni Hasan has paintings of hunting, fishing, craftsmen and a siege, and on the east wall a long cycle of wrestlers: 220 pairs, with one figure in each pair painted red and the other dark brown, so that the holds are clearly visible.

The cliffs of Dhar Tichitt in the south-western Sahara were inhabited by herders and farmers between about 2000 and 300 BC. The site may have been the main centre of a hierarchical society within the Tichitt culture. On the plateaus, drystone compounds with houses and granaries were built, sometimes along streets. The inhabitants grew pearl millet and are thought to be ancestors of the Soninke people.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the site was inhabited about 2000–300 BC and that the stone villages on the plateaus were built about 1400–300 BC. An earlier phase with mobile hunters and herders is dated to 2600–1900 BC.

summary.en: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is an Egyptian medical text and the oldest known treatise on surgery for injuries. It describes 48 cases of injuries, fractures, wounds, dislocations and tumours, and it differs from other Egyptian medical papyri in that it does not prescribe magic. The copy dates from about 1600 BC and probably comes from Thebes, but the original may date from the Old Kingdom.

caption.en: Columns 6 and 7 of the Edwin Smith Papyrus, which deal with injuries to the face. Image of the original. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: The Rhind Papyrus is one of the best-known examples of Egyptian mathematics. The scribe Ahmose copied it around 1550 BC, in year 33 of the Hyksos king Apepi, from an older original from the time of Pharaoh Amenemhat III. In the opening he promises “accurate reckoning” and knowledge of all things. The papyrus comes from Thebes and was bought in Luxor in 1858 by the Scottish antiquarian Alexander Henry Rhind.

caption.en: The left part of the first section on the front of the Rhind Papyrus, British Museum (EA 10057). Image of the original. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: Cyrene in present-day Libya was founded in 631 BC by colonists from Thera, today Santorini, led by Battus I. The city was first ruled by his dynasty, the Battiads, who grew rich and powerful thanks to new waves of immigrants and the export of horses and silphium, a medicinal plant.

text.en: Wikipedia's infobox gives 631 BC. The text says that the city was probably colonised by settlers from Thera in the late 7th century BC.

summary.en: Nuri is a Nubian necropolis on the west bank of the Nile in northern Sudan, where the kings and queens of Kush were buried. The pyramids were built over more than three centuries, from about 670 BC, when the oldest was built for King Taharqa, to about 310 BC. More than 20 pyramids still stand, and at its height there were probably 80 or more.

At the beginning of the Meroitic period, in the 3rd century BC, two scripts were developed to write Meroitic, the language of the Kingdom of Kush. Meroitic Cursive came from Egyptian Demotic and Meroitic Hieroglyphs from Egyptian hieroglyphs. The cursive accounts for about 90 percent of all inscriptions. Before the Meroitic period, Kushite names were written with Egyptian hieroglyphs.

Gonur Depe in present-day Turkmenistan is an archaeological site dated to 2400–1600 BC. The fortified northern part, with a large palace, temples, water reservoirs and a royal burial ground, was in use around 2400–1900 BC.

Around 2300 BC construction of the city of Lothal in Gujarat begins. It belonged to the Indus civilisation and lay on a trade route between the cities of Sindh and the Kathiawar peninsula. According to India's archaeological authority (ASI), Lothal may have had one of the world's earliest known docks, connecting the city to an old course of the Sabarmati River.

text.en: Wikipedia also cites scholars who argue that Lothal was a fairly small town and that the "dock" was mainly an irrigation tank.

summary.en: The Sintashta culture of the Southern Urals is dated to about 2200–1900 BC. It had fortified settlements, extensive copper and bronze working and graves with weapons. The earliest known chariots come from here: several graves hold impressions of spoked wheels, and radiocarbon dates suggest they existed before 2000 BC.

text.en: Wikipedia's infobox gives 2200–1900 BC. According to a later dating cited by Wikipedia, the cemeteries were used until about 1770 BC.

summary.en: Around 1800 BC the clay tablet Plimpton 322 is written in cuneiform in Babylonia. It contains numbers that form Pythagorean triples, the sides of right-angled triangles. The tablet is about 13 centimetres wide and is now at Columbia University in New York.

text.en: That the tablet comes from Senkereh, ancient Larsa, rests on the word of the antiquities dealer Edgar Banks, who sold it. Comparisons with dated tablets from Larsa suggest the years 1822–1784 BC.

caption.en: The clay tablet Plimpton 322, a Babylonian table of numbers. Photographer unknown. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Under the Shang king Wu Ding, the results of the royal family's divinations are carved into ox shoulder bones and turtle shells, the earliest body of Chinese writing. The inscriptions from his reign have been radiocarbon dated to 1254–1197 BC. Most of the roughly 150,000 inscriptions found come from Yinxu, the last Shang capital near present-day Anyang.

caption.en: Oracle bones with inscriptions from the Shang dynasty, found at Yinxu near Anyang in China. Photo: Gary Lee Todd, 2018. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: The Phoenician alphabet is conventionally dated from about 1050 BC and was used until 146 BC. It is written from right to left and has signs only for consonants. Phoenician inscriptions have been found in former Phoenician cities and colonies around the Mediterranean, for example in Byblos and Carthage.

text.en: The year 1050 BC is a convention. The oldest known inscriptions are from the 10th century BC, and the dating of Ahiram's epitaph in Byblos, which shows the fully developed script, is disputed.

summary.en: From about 747 BC to 61 BC, for some 700 years, Babylonian scribes keep diaries in cuneiform. They record celestial phenomena, predictions, weather, commodity prices and political events. The systematic records began under King Nabonassar and made it possible to discover a repeating 18-year cycle of lunar eclipses.

Among other things, Lydia in western Anatolia is remembered for the world's first coins. Its electrum coins, made of a mix of gold and silver, are some of the oldest ever found and date from roughly the 7th century BC. Sardis was the kingdom's capital, and its only city.

text.en: When the first coins were struck is debated: the dates range from 700 to 550 BC. The most common view is that they were struck at the beginning of the reign of King Alyattes. The source contradicts itself about Alyattes: in the section on the coins his reign is given as about 591–560 BC, but elsewhere it says he died in 585 BC. According to the source, the largest share of the early electrum coins was struck at Sardis; the point is placed at Sardis, the capital of Lydia.

summary.en: According to Jain tradition, Mahavira is born in 599 BC into a princely family in Kundagrama, near Vaishali in present-day Bihar. He is regarded as the 24th tirthankara of Jainism, one of its spiritual teachers. Scholars agree that he is a historical person, but not on when he lived.

text.en: The years 599–527 BC are the traditional dating of the Svetambara branch. According to the Digambara branch he died in 510 BC. Historians date his life uncertainly and later, perhaps to the 6th or early 5th century BC.

summary.en: In the Pazyryk valley in the Altai mountains, Scythian-type burial mounds are built with wooden chambers under stone cairns. Water seeped into the tombs in antiquity and froze, so rare objects of organic material were preserved in the permafrost: felt hangings, Chinese silk, the earliest known pile carpet and horses with elaborate trappings.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the tombs to the 4th and 3rd centuries BC, but also mentions tombs from the 5th century BC at Pazyryk.
