summary.en: The Maurya emperor Ashoka, who ruled 268–232 BC, has more than thirty inscriptions carved on pillars, boulders and cave walls across much of the Indian subcontinent. They are the first tangible evidence of Buddhism. One of them, at Girnar, names the Greek king Antiochus among those who received Ashoka's medical care.

Around 256 BC the state of Qin builds the Dujiangyan system on the Min River for irrigation and flood control. Through a narrow opening in the mountain, water is led out over the Chengdu Plain. The engineer Li Bing led the work. The system is still in use.

Between the 3rd century BC and the 1st century AD, the texts now called the Dead Sea Scrolls are written, mostly in Hebrew but also in Aramaic and Greek. They were found in 1946–1956 in eleven caves near Khirbet Qumran in the Judaean Desert. In all, 981 separate manuscripts have been pieced together.

caption.en: Part of the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, one of the Dead Sea Scrolls. Photo: Ardon Bar Hama. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Óc Eo in the Mekong Delta is a busy port of the kingdom of Funan from the 2nd century BC to the 12th century AD. Excavations have found pottery, tools, jewellery, moulds for jewellery, coins and religious statues. The site may have been the port that the Greeks and Romans called Cattigara.

For about a thousand years, one of the largest Iron Age settlements in the Nordic countries lay at Uppåkra. It was an economic, political and religious centre, with trade, crafts and a cult house. The site lost its importance at about the time Lund was founded five kilometres away.

text.en: Den Store Danske has the settlement begin around 100 BC and English Wikipedia in the last century BC. Swedish Wikipedia gives around AD 100 to after 900. The end is given as the end of the Viking Age or the 990s.

summary.en: Neanderthals lived in Europe and in western and central Asia. According to the sources they died out in western Eurasia about 39,000 years ago, after living at the same time as Homo sapiens in Europe for several thousand years. A Neanderthal tooth from Bawa Yawan in the Zagros Mountains is 43,600–41,500 years old. Neanderthals and Homo sapiens had children together, and traces of this are found in the genomes of all people outside Africa studied so far.

text.en: The extinction about 39,000 years ago (Harvati and Reyes-Centeno 2022), or 40,000–37,000 years ago (Heydari-Guran et al. 2021), is based on finds in western Eurasia. In Central Asia and Siberia it may have been different. The species is older than the timeline, which begins at 100,000 BC.

summary.en: Denisovans are a group of humans first identified through DNA from a small bone of a finger or toe in Denisova Cave. Denisovan DNA is found there in layers from about 250,000 years ago, and the oldest fossils from about 200,000 years ago. A rib from Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau is 48,000–32,000 years old, the youngest find in the sources. Neanderthals also lived in Denisova Cave, and one of the finds comes from a child of a Neanderthal and a Denisovan.

text.en: Denisovans have no formal species name, but several names have been proposed. Some researchers see fossils from China, including the one named Homo longi, as possible Denisovans (Harvati and Reyes-Centeno 2022). The group existed before the start of the timeline at 100,000 BC. The span ends at the youngest possible age of the layer with the rib; it shows that they were present then, not when they disappeared.

summary.en: Homo floresiensis was a short human species on the island of Flores. The finds in the cave of Liang Bua are 100,000–60,000 years old. Ancestors with even smaller jaws and teeth lived on the same island about 700,000 years ago, according to finds at Mata Menge.

text.en: The review counts Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis as the two recognised human species on islands in Southeast Asia. That the arrival of Homo sapiens on Flores had to do with the species’ disappearance is a hypothesis.

summary.en: Homo luzonensis is known from finds in Callao Cave on the island of Luzon in the Philippines: a foot bone found in 2007 and twelve further finds from the same layer, from at least three individuals. The foot bone is dated by uranium-series dating to at least about 67,000 years; the age is a minimum age, so the bone may be older. According to a later article, the finds are at least 50,000 and perhaps more than 100,000 years old. In 2019 the finds were described as a separate species.

text.en: One review counts Homo luzonensis as a recognised species, but according to other authors the finds are fragmentary and difficult to assign to a species.

summary.en: According to the researchers, a tooth from the cave of Gua Dagang at Niah on Borneo has features usually found in archaic humans but not in Homo sapiens. It is about 55,000–52,000 years old according to optical dating, that is, from just before or at the same time as Homo sapiens arrived at Niah. Which species it belongs to has not been established.

Homo erectus was the first human species in Island Southeast Asia and reached Java more than 1.5 million years ago. At Ngandong in Central Java, twelve skull caps and two shin bones of the species were found in 1931–1933, in a bone bed about 20 metres above the Solo River. According to a model based on 52 age estimates, the bone bed is 117,000–108,000 years old. Ngandong is the last known place where Homo erectus lived.

text.en: Homo erectus is included as a borderline case: the bone bed is older than the start of the timeline at 100,000 BC. Its age has long been disputed. Datings from 1996 gave 35,000–50,000 years. Indriati et al. 2011 obtained two results that do not agree: on average about 546,000 years with argon, and with ESR and uranium-series dating about 143,000 years for the oldest sample that met all the model criteria, probably a minimum age. The span of 117,000–108,000 years comes from Rizal et al. 2020 and is repeated by Curnoe et al. 2025. No source gives the coordinates of the find site. The point is read from the map in figure 1 of Indriati et al. 2011, about 0.8 km north-east of the grid intersection where the map gives the coordinates, and is approximate.

summary.en: At the Madjedbebe rock shelter in northern Australia, the oldest layer with dense traces of people is dated to about 65,000–53,000 years ago, by optical dating and radiocarbon. The layer contains charcoal, ground ochre, grinding stones and more than 10,000 stone artefacts. That would be an early trace of Homo sapiens in the region.

text.en: Questions have been raised about how reliable the dating is, because of possible complications in the sequence of layers (Curnoe et al. 2025).

summary.en: According to the source, the finds at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco are the oldest currently counted as part of our own lineage, Homo sapiens. They are about 300,000 years old. The face, jaw and teeth resemble those of people today, but the braincase lacks the rounded shape typical of modern humans.

text.en: The early finds do not have all the features of later Homo sapiens. According to the source, whether they should count as a separate species or as early Homo sapiens is an open question.

summary.en: The Omo I remains were found in the late 1960s in the Omo valley in southern Ethiopia and are classified as Homo sapiens. A layer of ash from a volcanic eruption lies above the layer with the finds, and a new dating of the eruption shows that the finds are at least about 233,000 years old, with a margin of error of 22,000 years. They are among the oldest known finds of Homo sapiens in eastern Africa.

text.en: Earlier, about 197,000 years was the age usually given. The new age is a minimum age, so the finds may be older (Vidal et al. 2022). Omo II looks more archaic than Omo I and is sometimes considered distinct from Omo I, possibly an earlier population within the Homo sapiens lineage (Harvati and Reyes-Centeno 2022).

summary.en: The finds from Herto in the Afar rift in Ethiopia were discovered in the late 1990s and are classified as Homo sapiens. Their age is usually given as about 160,000–155,000 years.

text.en: The age depends on how ash layers at different sites are linked to each other, and those links have been questioned. According to Vidal et al. 2022, the ash layer that gives Omo I its minimum age cannot be used to give Herto a minimum age. The same study nevertheless finds that its results are consistent with about 160,000 years and that the Herto finds are considerably younger than Omo I.

summary.en: The finds in the caves of Qafzeh and Skhūl in present-day Israel are about 130,000–90,000 years old. According to the source, they may belong to early Homo sapiens who spread out of Africa long before the major dispersal out of Africa, which the source places at about 60,000 years ago.

text.en: The source counts the finds as possible representatives of Homo sapiens. Not all early finds have all the features typical of modern humans, and many are incomplete.

summary.en: In the cave of Panga ya Saidi in Kenya, researchers have found part of the skeleton of a child aged 2.5–3 years. The child lay curled up in a pit that had been dug on purpose and filled in again. The grave is about 78,000 years old and the oldest known burial in Africa. According to the source the skeleton is consistent with Homo sapiens, but the teeth have some archaic features.

In the deepest layers of Tam Pà Ling cave in northern Laos, researchers have found part of a frontal bone and part of a shin bone from Homo sapiens. The frontal bone is about 70,000 years old and the shin bone about 77,000 years. The bones are dated through the layers and the animal teeth around them. The finds suggest that Homo sapiens reached Southeast Asia early, in a dispersal that according to the source may not have lasted.

Bones from the Ilsenhöhle cave at Ranis in Germany come from Homo sapiens and are about 45,000 years old (radiocarbon dated to about 49,000–42,000 years ago). Their genomes show that several of them were related, among them a mother and her daughter, and that a person from Zlatý kůň in Czechia was a fifth- or sixth-degree relative. They belonged to a small, isolated group that according to the source has no descendants among people today.
At Al Wusta in Saudi Arabia a small bone from a finger or toe has been found that is about 90,000 years old. The source counts it among the early finds of Homo sapiens outside Africa.

In several caves in southern and central China, finds, mainly teeth, have been counted as possible early Homo sapiens. The dates are 120,000–80,000 years at Fuyan Cave, 100,000–80,000 years at Huanglongdong, 127,000–70,000 years at Lunadong and 116,000–106,000 years at Zhirendong. If they are right, they point to an early dispersal that possibly failed.

text.en: The finds are hotly debated. Sun et al. made new datings at several of the sites and questioned the high ages, among them that of the Zhiren 3 jaw. Other researchers have in turn pointed to problems in that study: inaccurate radiocarbon ages, a sampled tooth wrongly assigned to the genus Homo, possible contamination in the genetic analyses and uncertain find contexts (Freidline et al. 2023).

summary.en: According to the source, a partial skull from Florisbad in South Africa is one of the possible early finds of Homo sapiens in Africa. It is more than 180,000 years old.

text.en: The skull has also been given its own species name, Homo helmei (Dreyer 1935), but the source counts it among the possible early Homo sapiens. Not all early finds have all the features typical of modern humans, and many are incomplete.

summary.en: The Misliya 1 find from a cave on Mount Carmel in present-day Israel is about 180,000 years old. It has been described as one of the earliest finds of Homo sapiens outside Africa, at least 60,000 years older than the finds at Skhūl and Qafzeh.

text.en: The source counts the finds as possible representatives of Homo sapiens. Not all early finds have all the features typical of modern humans, and many are incomplete.

summary.en: The Apidima 1 find from a cave in southern Greece is about 210,000 years old or older. It has been described as one of the earliest finds of Homo sapiens outside Africa.

text.en: The source counts the finds as possible representatives of Homo sapiens. Not all early finds have all the features typical of modern humans, and many are incomplete.

summary.en: In Xianrendong Cave in southern China, sherds of clay pots have been found in layers that are 20,000–19,000 years old according to radiocarbon dating. This is among the oldest known pottery. It was made by mobile hunter-gatherers during the coldest part of the last ice age, at least 10,000 years before farming arrived. Burn marks on many sherds suggest that the pots were used for cooking.

text.en: It is the layers around the sherds that have been dated, not the sherds themselves. Wikipedia’s infobox gives 20,000–17,800 years, without a source of its own. Wikipedia also mentions early rice cultivation, but the scientific paper says that the pottery is thousands of years older than farming.

summary.en: Çatalhöyük in southern Anatolia was a settlement from around 7500 to 5600 BC. The houses of mud brick stood close together without streets. People entered through openings in the roof by ladders, and the roofs served as streets. The dead were buried under the floors. There are wall paintings and more than 2,500 clay figurines. The inhabitants grew several kinds of wheat and peas, and obsidian tools were an important craft. The site became a World Heritage Site in 2012.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the start as around 7500 BC in the introduction but around 7100 BC in the infobox. 5600 BC is the end for the eastern mound; the western mound was inhabited afterwards. Older estimates spoke of 5,000–7,000 inhabitants, but newer research gives 600–800 people in a typical year. That the society was egalitarian or worshipped a mother goddess are disputed interpretations.

summary.en: Around 8000 BC a tower of undressed stone was built in Jericho, about 8.5 metres high and with a staircase inside. It stood within the wall around the settlement of Tell es-Sultan and was built before pottery was made there. The archaeologist Kathleen Kenyon excavated the tower in 1952–1958. What it was used for is unknown; one interpretation links it to the shadow at sunset on midsummer. Tell es-Sultan became a World Heritage Site in 2023.

text.en: No dating method is given, and the date partly rests on a newspaper article. The pre-pottery phase at the site lasted about 8500–7500 BC. The Wikipedia articles disagree about how long the tower was the tallest building and whether it is the oldest tower, so those claims are left out.

summary.en: In the cave of Leang Karampuang on the island of Sulawesi there is a painting of human-like figures that appear to interact with a wild pig. A thin layer of calcite has formed on top of the paint, and it is at least 51,200 years old according to uranium-series dating. The painting is therefore at least that old, and it is one of the oldest known examples of pictures that tell something. The same karst area has about 300 caves with paintings, among them Leang Tedongnge with a life-size pig at least 45,500 years old. The painters were probably Homo sapiens.

text.en: It is the calcite on top of the paint that has been dated, so the painting may be older. The measurement gave 53,500 ± 2,300 years, and the secure minimum age is 51,200 years; Wikipedia sometimes gives the first figure as if it were certain. A hand stencil on the island of Muna, south-east of Sulawesi, was reported in 2026 to be at least 67,800 years old. It does not depict a human or an animal, so Karampuang is still among the oldest known pictures of humans and animals.

summary.en: Lascaux Cave in south-western France has hundreds of paintings of large animals, mostly horses and then deer, but also aurochs and bison. There is only one human figure. The colours were made from minerals such as ochre and manganese compounds. The paintings are most often estimated to be 17,000–22,000 years old, but this is still debated. The entrance was found in 1940 by an 18-year-old boy. The cave has been closed to visitors since 1963 to protect the paintings, and replicas are shown today.

text.en: Wikipedia gives no dating method, and the span of 17,000–22,000 years rests on weak sources. The same article says 19,000 years elsewhere, and Wikidata gives the 16th millennium BC without a source. What the paintings meant, for example hunting magic or rituals, is a matter of interpretation.

summary.en: Newgrange is a large Neolithic passage tomb on a ridge above the River Boyne in Ireland, built around 3100 BC according to radiocarbon dates. At the winter solstice the rising sun shines through an opening above the entrance, along the passage and into the chamber for about 17 minutes. White quartz and dark stones were brought from about 50 kilometres away. Both burnt and unburnt human bones have been found in the passage. What the tomb was used for is not known, but it is thought to have had religious significance.

text.en: Some researchers date the construction to 3000–2500 BC instead of around 3100 BC. Today the light arrives a few minutes after sunrise and no longer reaches the back wall, because the tilt of the Earth’s axis has changed. That the light was intended is considered likely, but what it was meant to signify is speculation. An interpretation that an elite with royal traits built the tomb is disputed.

summary.en: Skara Brae in Orkney is a Neolithic village of stone. According to radiocarbon dates it was begun around 3180 BC and abandoned around 2500 BC. The houses share a layout with a hearth in the middle, beds on both sides and a dresser opposite the door, and the furniture is made of stone. The inhabitants kept cattle, pigs and sheep, ate fish and shellfish and probably grew barley. The village came to light in 1850, when a storm blew the soil off a mound.

title.en: Why the village was abandoned is unknown

text.en: A colder and wetter climate may have driven the inhabitants away. The story of a sudden storm that buried the village is called a myth by another researcher: the sand covered the village gradually, after it had already been abandoned.

summary.en: Ötzi is a man who died in the Alps between 3359 and 3105 BC, according to radiocarbon dates. His body was naturally preserved in the ice and was found in 1991 by two tourists at about 3,210 metres, just inside Italy’s border. He carried a copper axe, a flint dagger and a bow. Traces in his teeth suggest that he grew up north of Bolzano. X-rays revealed an arrowhead in his left shoulder, so he was probably killed by another person. He is on display today in the archaeological museum in Bolzano.

text.en: Wikipedia states that he died around 3230 BC, a year within the span, and gives both “about 5,100” and “5,300” years ago. How he died is still being investigated: Wikipedia says he probably bled to death, but a clinical study from 2025 considers heavy bleeding unlikely and suggests that he lived for several hours after the arrow struck, with altitude, cold and exertion also contributing.

summary.en: About 74,000 years ago one of the largest known explosive volcanic eruptions on Earth took place where Lake Toba on Sumatra lies today. The lake is the water-filled caldera left by the eruption. Argon–argon dating gives about 73,900–73,700 years ago. Ash fell over the Indian subcontinent, and tiny glass shards from the eruption have been found as far away as South Africa, Ethiopia and Lake Malawi. Neanderthals and Denisovans survived the eruption.

text.en: The theory that the eruption caused a volcanic winter that almost wiped out humanity is disputed, and some researchers consider it disproven. Stone tools in southern India are very similar below and above the ash, but at another site in India there are signs that the population fell sharply. The climate effect is also debated: models give a few years of strong cooling, while other data suggest a small or a longer effect.

summary.en: Mehrgarh is a Neolithic settlement near the Bolan Pass in Pakistan and one of the earliest known sites in South Asia with traces of farming and herding. In the oldest period there was no pottery. People grew wheat and barley and kept sheep, goats and cattle, and the zebu, native to the plain, was soon domesticated. New radiocarbon dates on tooth enamel from the graves show that people settled there around 5200–4900 BC.

text.en: The older dating, which Wikipedia gives, placed the start before 7000 BC, and one study mentions as early as 8500 BC. The new study from 2025 dates tooth enamel from 23 graves and excludes the older dates, which were made on charcoal with older methods. Researchers also disagree about whether farming arrived with migrants from the west or arose on the spot. Two sources place the site about 20 kilometres apart.

summary.en: The Botai culture in northern Kazakhstan had large settlements with pit houses, and most of the refuse is horse bones. There are teeth with wear that may come from bits, and traces of corrals and horse dung. Other researchers think the horses were wild and hunted. Genetic studies show that today’s domestic horses do not descend from Botai’s horses, which are instead related to Przewalski’s horse.

text.en: Wikipedia gives both 3700–3500 and 3700–3100 BC. Researchers disagree about whether the horses at Botai were domesticated or hunted, and the same article contradicts itself on the question. According to a genetic study from 2021, today’s domestic horses come from the steppe by the lower Volga and Don and spread from there from around 2200–2000 BC.

summary.en: The Ishango bone is a dark brown, curved bone about 10 centimetres long with a piece of quartz fixed at one end. It was found in 1950 at Ishango, where the Semliki River flows out of Lake Edward. The bone has 168 engraved notches in three columns. They have been interpreted as tally marks, a counting aid or a lunar calendar, but others think the notches simply gave a better grip. The bone is about 20,000 years old and is kept in Brussels today.

text.en: The bone was first estimated at 9000–6500 BC, and other analyses have given up to 44,000 years. Today about 20,000 years is given, but the sources write both 20,000–18,000 BC and 18,000–20,000 years ago. The dating is debated because volcanic activity has disturbed the carbon isotopes. Older engraved bones exist, so it is not the world’s oldest counting tool.

summary.en: According to radiocarbon dates on the skeletons, the Jebel Sahaba cemetery on the Nile is at least 13,400 years old. Of 61 people examined, 41 had at least one healed or unhealed injury, and 16 had injuries from the time of death, including children. Most injuries come from arrows and spears, and stone points are still lodged in several skeletons. That the same people have both healed and fresh injuries suggests repeated violence between groups, perhaps in raids and ambushes, rather than a single battle. The cemetery was excavated in the 1960s.

text.en: The 2021 study gives 13,400–18,600 years in one place and 13,400–18,200 years in another. An older date from 1988 has been rejected because the samples were poorly preserved. The site has often been called a war, but the study rejects the interpretation as a single war. That climate change triggered the violence is the authors’ interpretation. According to Wikipedia, the cemetery now lies under Lake Nasser.

summary.en: Wild potato species grow from the southern United States to southern Chile, but the cultivated potato has a single origin in southern Peru, according to genetic studies. It was domesticated around Lake Titicaca about 10,000–7,000 years ago, according to estimates. Potato starch is found on stone tools in the Titicaca Basin from around 3400–1600 BC, and the oldest securely attested tuber comes from Ancón on the coast of Peru, around 2500 BC. About 3,000 varieties are grown in the Andes today.

text.en: The span of 10,000–7,000 years ago (8000–5000 BC) is an estimate, and the source Wikipedia relies on could not be opened. The genetic study gives the place but no time. Direct finds appear only several thousand years later. That more than 99 per cent of today’s varieties descend from a subspecies in southern Chile applies to today’s varieties, not to the first domestication.

summary.en: Fishers and gatherers on the coast of northern Chile began to mummify their dead around 5050 BC. These are the oldest known deliberately preserved human bodies in the world. The bodies were rebuilt and reinforced, shaped with clay and given wigs and mineral paint. Men, women and children were preserved, not just an elite. Around 90 per cent of their food came from the sea. The custom lasted about 3,000 years, and the sites became a World Heritage Site in 2021.

text.en: The sources give the start as around 5050 or 5000 BC and the end as around 1800 or 1300 BC. The oldest naturally preserved body is older, around 7020 BC. The article on the culture says the mummies go back to around 7000 BC and does not distinguish between natural and deliberate mummies. No dating method is given for 5050 BC.

summary.en: A cave in Patagonia holds more than 2,000 handprints, most of them painted as stencils around the hand. The images were made in several phases from around 7300 BC to around AD 700. This has been shown by radiocarbon dating, by remains of bone tubes through which the paint was sprayed, and by a piece of painted rock wall that fell into the layers. Almost all the hands are left hands: 829 against 31. The oldest style shows hunter-gatherers hunting guanacos. The cave became a World Heritage Site in 1999.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the start of the art as around 7300 BC. Wikidata gives 7350 BC, without a source. That the cave has the oldest cave paintings in South America is a claim by two researchers, not a general conclusion.

summary.en: The wild ancestor of maize, teosinte, grows in the Balsas valley in southern Mexico. In the rock shelter of Xihuatoxtla near Iguala, grinding stones have been found with starch grains and phytoliths from maize. Charcoal in the same layer is about 8,700 years old according to radiocarbon dating, so maize was there by then at the latest. Genetic studies suggest that maize was domesticated about 9,000 years ago. A domesticated squash was present just as early. The growers were small groups who moved with the seasons.

text.en: The archaeology gives a minimum age: maize was at Xihuatoxtla by about 8,700 years ago at the latest (the charcoal is calibrated to 8,990–8,610 years before 1950). The genetics point to about 9,000 years ago. The span shows both. The location is approximate: the sources only say that the rock shelter is near Iguala.

summary.en: Watson Brake in Louisiana is the oldest known mound complex in North America. Eleven mounds joined by ridges form an oval almost 900 feet (about 270 metres) across. According to 27 radiocarbon dates, building began around 3500 BC and went on for about 500 years, and the site was abandoned around 2800 BC. The builders were hunter-gatherers, not farmers, and lived on fish, shellfish and seeds. The finds changed researchers’ picture of who could build large structures.

About 13,800–11,400 years ago some 35 genera of large animals died out in North America. Around 72 per cent of the large mammal species in North America and 83 per cent in South America disappeared, along with every mammal weighing more than a tonne. In the Americas it happened almost at the same time, within 3,000 years at most. This was roughly when people arrived in the Americas and when the cold Younger Dryas period began. Bison, wolves and grizzly bears survived. The La Brea tar pits have yielded fossils of mammoths, sabre-toothed cats and giant ground sloths, among others.

text.en: Researchers have long disagreed about the cause: human hunting, climate change or both. Most think that humans contributed, but the question is not settled. The time limits are also uncertain, as the radiocarbon record in North America has been called inadequate. The span refers to North America; in South America the extinctions came after people arrived there about 15,000 years ago.

summary.en: Chauvet Cave in southern France has some of the best-preserved figurative cave paintings in the world. It holds hundreds of images of animals from at least 13 species, with unusually many predators such as cave lions, leopards, bears and cave hyenas. The artists scraped the walls clean and engraved around the outlines to give depth. According to a model based on 259 radiocarbon dates, people visited the cave in two periods, 37,000–33,500 and 31,000–28,000 years ago, and most of the black drawings belong to the earlier one. The cave was found in 1994.

text.en: A study from 2012 gives about 32,000–30,000 years ago for the earlier period. Some researchers consider the paintings younger: a style-based dating places the red paintings in the Gravettian and the black ones in the early Magdalenian, and others have questioned where the charcoal came from and whether the samples are contaminated. Other researchers have replied to the criticism.

summary.en: The Lion-man is a 31-centimetre figure in mammoth ivory with a human body and the head of a cave lion. It was found in the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in southern Germany in 1939, in more than 200 pieces. The Second World War began a week later, and the pieces lay forgotten in the museum in Ulm for about 30 years. The layer in which it lay is 41,000–35,000 years old according to radiocarbon dating. It is among the oldest known works of art of its kind.

text.en: It is the layer and the bones next to the figure that have been dated, not the ivory. The article on the cave gives 40,000–35,000 years in one place and 41,000–35,000 years in another. English Wikipedia calls the figure the oldest confirmed statue, but German Wikipedia only says that it is among the oldest and dates a figure from Hohle Fels to the same time.

summary.en: Where the southern North Sea lies today, a large land area existed after the Ice Age between Britain, the Netherlands, Germany and Jutland: Doggerland. As the ice melted, the sea rose and drowned the land step by step, first into low islands and then completely, between about 8000 and 5000 BC. Britain became an island. Dogger Bank was one of the last islands. In 1931 a trawler brought up a barbed point made of antler, and seismic surveys have mapped rivers and lakes on the seabed.

text.en: The role of the Storegga tsunami (around 6200 BC) is disputed. One hypothesis says it drowned the last coastal strip, one study says that only low islands remained, and the article on the Storegga Slide says the tsunami was not the reason the last remnants disappeared. The sources also differ on when Britain was cut off from the continent: around 6500 BC or only at the time of the slide. Dogger Bank was drowned later than the rest, so the marker does not show where it began.

summary.en: Near Varna in Bulgaria an excavator operator found a Copper Age cemetery in 1972. The graves date from 4569–4340 BC according to radiocarbon dating. The 294 graves held objects of gold and copper, pottery and blades of flint and obsidian, in all about 3,000 gold objects weighing some 6 kilograms. A single grave, number 43, held more gold than has been found in the rest of the world from the same time. Some graves have no skeleton, only grave goods. Copper from Bulgaria’s mountains and shells from the Mediterranean suggest long-distance trade.

text.en: Wikipedia’s introduction dates the gold to 4600–4200 BC, the section on chronology to 4569–4340 BC. The Varna gold is often called the oldest in the world, but the source itself says that other Bulgarian finds are considered just as old and that Varna is usually named because the find is the largest and most varied.

summary.en: In Blombos Cave on the south coast of South Africa more than 8,000 pieces of ochre have been found. Some are deliberately engraved, and two pieces have a pattern of crossing and parallel lines. The cave also held more than 70 pierced shells with wear marks showing that they were strung on a thread and worn as beads. The layers with the engraved pieces and most of the beads are about 75,000–72,000 years old according to optical dating (OSL). The finds are early traces of symbolic thinking in Homo sapiens.

text.en: The dating was criticised on methodological grounds in 2013, but according to the source other methods (thermoluminescence, uranium–thorium and ESR) agree with the optical dating. The whole sequence of layers in the cave is about 101,000–70,000 years old, and some of the engraved ochre pieces reported in 2009 come from older layers.

summary.en: About 14,600–5,000 years ago North Africa was much wetter than today. Grass, trees and lakes covered large parts of the Sahara. Changes in the Earth’s orbit and tilt, the vegetation and less dust strengthened the African monsoon. There were two dry interruptions, during the Younger Dryas and about 8,200 years ago. People settled in the Sahara, hunted and gathered and later kept cattle, goats and sheep, and they left rock art behind. As it dried out, people gradually moved to places with more reliable water, such as the Nile valley.

text.en: On the same page the start is given as about 14,600–14,500 or 15,000–14,500 years ago, and Wikidata gives around 13500 BC. The end varied with place: it came step by step from north to south, about 6,000–5,000 years ago in much of North Africa but 4,500–3,500 years ago in East Africa and later still nearer the equator. The central Sahara was desert by 2,700 years ago at the latest. The marker is in the middle of the Sahara; the period applied to the whole region.

summary.en: Nabta Playa was a seasonal lake in the Nubian Desert, about 100 kilometres west of Abu Simbel, when the Sahara was greener. People had seasonal camps there and later larger settlements with deep wells. From around 5500 BC cattle were buried in clay-lined chambers under stone mounds. Around 4800 BC a small stone circle was built with narrow stones roughly aligned with sunrise at the summer solstice, near the time when the rains usually came.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the stone circle to around 4800 BC in the text but to around 4000 BC in a picture caption, and no dating method is given. The name “calendar circle” may be misleading: UNESCO’s listing speaks of hypothetical alignments with the sun and stars. Whether the early cattle were domesticated is disputed.

summary.en: Ounjougou is a complex of more than a hundred sites in the Yamé valley on the Bandiagara plateau in Mali. It has the oldest finds of pottery in Africa, from the first half of the 10th millennium BC, before 9400 BC. The pottery, mostly small bowls with impressed decoration, appeared when the monsoon returned after the Younger Dryas and an open grassland savanna grew up. The region is counted among the earliest where pottery was invented independently, together with East Asia.

text.en: The dating comes from Wikipedia, which is based on Huysecom et al. 2009 (calibrated radiocarbon dates). That article could not be opened. Wikidata gives around 9500 BC, but with Wikipedia as its source, so it is not an independent second source. The sites are spread out, and the marker is approximate.

summary.en: The Younger Dryas was the last cold period of the most recent ice age, about 10900–9700 BC. The Northern Hemisphere cooled quickly, by about 3 degrees in North America, 2–6 degrees in Europe and up to 10 degrees in Greenland, while the Southern Hemisphere grew warmer. The period is named after the mountain avens, Dryas octopetala, whose fossils are common in Scandinavian layers from the time. It ended with rapid warming, and the Holocene, the present warm period, began.

text.en: Researchers agree that the ocean currents in the Atlantic weakened sharply, but not why: meltwater from a large ice-dammed lake in North America, volcanic eruptions or something else. The hypothesis of an impact from space is rejected by most experts. Wikidata gives 10950–9750 BC, which is the same figures counted from the year 1950. The cold did not begin at the same time everywhere; in East Asia it came several hundred years later.

summary.en: At Kuk in the New Guinea highlands, about 1,550 metres above sea level, people dug ditches to drain the wetland and grow crops, from about 9,000 years ago. Among the crops was the native taro, and later there are traces of bananas and sugar cane. Kuk is one of the places where people developed farming on their own, without learning it from others. The site became a World Heritage Site in 2008.

text.en: The source dates the ditches to about 9,000 years ago but gives no dating method. The cultivation of bananas and sugar cane is given on the same page as both 6,900–6,400 and 6,950–6,550 years ago.

summary.en: A lava flow from the Budj Bim volcano in south-eastern Australia created large wetlands. There the Gunditjmara people built a system of ponds, channels and stone walls that guided the water from Darlot Creek and trapped eels. One of five trap systems at Lake Condah is about 6,600 years old according to radiocarbon dating, so the system is at least that old. Budj Bim became a World Heritage Site in 2019.

text.en: The introduction on the same page says the system was built up to 8,000 years ago, but without a reference. The radiocarbon date, 6,600 years, applies to one of five trap systems and is a minimum age.

summary.en: Gabarnmung is a rock shelter with paintings on the land of the Jawoyn people in Arnhem Land in northern Australia. On a painted piece of rock that had fallen from the ceiling lay ash that is about 28,000 years old according to radiocarbon dating. The ceiling must therefore have been painted more than 28,000 years ago. That makes it Australia’s oldest securely dated rock painting. The paintings show fish, wallabies, crocodiles, people and spirit figures, among other things.

text.en: It is the ash on the piece of rock that has been dated (27,631 ± 717 calibrated years before 1950), not the paint. The painting is therefore at least that old but may be older. People used the rock shelter even earlier, at least 44,000 years ago.

summary.en: A bone fragment from Denisova Cave in the Altai, known as Denisova 11, comes from the child of a Neanderthal and a Denisovan. The fragment lay in layers deposited about 150,000–80,000 years ago, and its age is estimated at 118,000–79,000 years. Researchers have found fossils of both Denisovans and Neanderthals in the cave. The find shows that the two groups met and had children together.

In Baishiya Karst Cave, 3,280 metres above sea level on the north-eastern Tibetan Plateau, a lower jaw and a rib from Denisovans have been found, as well as Denisovan DNA in the sediment layers. According to the source, Denisovans were present in the cave from at least 160,000 years ago, and the rib comes from a layer that is 48,000–32,000 years old. Marks on the animal bones in the cave suggest that the Denisovans made use of meat, marrow and hides and made tools from bone.

text.en: The span ends at the youngest possible age of the layer with the rib. It shows that Denisovans were present in the cave then, not when they disappeared. The rib has been linked to the Denisovans through its proteins.

summary.en: In White Sands National Park in New Mexico there are human footprints in layers by the shore of an ancient lake, together with tracks of large Ice Age animals. The layers are dated to about 23,500–21,700 years ago by radiocarbon dating of seeds and pollen. That would mean that people were in North America when the ice sheets were at their largest. There are also straight drag marks that the researchers interpret as traces of a travois, a frame of poles pulled along the ground.

text.en: The first dating, about 23,000–21,000 years (Bennett et al. 2021), was based on seeds of an aquatic plant, and such seeds can give ages that are too old. The researchers have since dated pollen and the sediments themselves and stand by the age (Pigati et al. 2023, Springer et al. 2026). All three sources come from the same research group, so there is no independent source here.

summary.en: At Monte Verde in Chile there is a campsite that according to its excavators is about 14,500 years old. It has the remains of a long tent-like dwelling, hearths, human footprints, plants that were used, and objects of wood and stone. The site has long been regarded as one of the most secure early traces of people in South America, but an independent investigation from 2026 holds that it is at most about 8,200 years old.

text.en: The excavators date the campsite to about 14,500 years (Dillehay et al. 2015). An independent investigation (Surovell et al. 2026) found a layer of volcanic ash, dated to 11,000 years, beneath the layer with the campsite and concludes that the campsite cannot be older than 8,200–4,200 years. The excavators have also reported possible older traces, from between at least about 18,500 and 14,500 years ago and from a layer that is about 33,000 years old, but are themselves sceptical about the oldest layer.

summary.en: During the Bronze Age, roughly 1700–500 BC, people at Tanum in Bohuslän carve thousands of images into the bedrock, on some 600 rock surfaces along a stretch of 25 kilometres. The area became a World Heritage Site in 1994.

text.en: Swedish Wikipedia dates the carvings to 1700–500 BC. English Wikipedia gives only the Bronze Age in Scandinavia, roughly 1800–500 BC. The dates are approximate.

summary.en: The Clovis culture is the earliest archaeological culture that can be recognised across much of North America. It is dated to about 13,050–12,750 years ago, based on ten securely dated sites. The type site is at Blackwater Draw near Clovis in New Mexico, where stone tools were found together with mammoth bones in 1929. The people were mobile hunter-gatherers who hunted large animals, especially mammoths, and their points have a characteristic flute. For a long time many researchers thought they were the first people in the Americas, but because of older finds most researchers now reject that idea.

text.en: Wikipedia and Waters et al. (2020) give about 13,050–12,750 years ago. Other researchers extend the culture back to about 13,500 years ago, but those dates are not secure, and Wikidata gives a younger span without a source. The type site, Blackwater Draw, has no secure date itself. Most researchers now reject the idea that the Clovis people were the first in the Americas: the White Sands footprints (23,500–21,700 years ago), Cooper's Ferry (about 16,500 years ago) and Monte Verde (about 14,500 years ago) are older, but all three dates have been questioned. Missing finds do not mean that nobody was there.

summary.en: The Bantu expansion was a long series of prehistoric migrations. Peoples speaking Proto-Bantu spread from an area around the border between Cameroon and Nigeria across large parts of Central, East and Southern Africa, according to the source roughly between 4000 BC and AD 500. A western branch went south along the coast or the rivers through the Congo rainforest and reached central Angola around 500 BC. An eastern branch reached the area west of Lake Victoria at about the same time, and Bantu speakers reached South Africa perhaps as early as around AD 300. Along the way they absorbed, displaced and in some cases perhaps replaced the hunter-gatherers and herders who already lived there. The main evidence is that so many languages south of the equator resemble each other, together with archaeology and genetics.

text.en: Based on linguistics, the source states that the expansion took place about 6,000–1,500 years ago, that is, about 4000 BC–AD 500. A genetic study from 2023 of 1,487 Bantu speakers from 143 populations in 14 African countries instead concluded that the expansion occurred in West Africa about 4,000 years ago. The early stages rest on reconstructions from languages, archaeology and genetics, not on written sources, so the dates are uncertain.

summary.en: Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great, came from Persis and was king of Anshan under the Medes. He rebelled against the Median king Astyages, his maternal grandfather. In 550 BC he defeated the Medes, captured Astyages and took the capital Ecbatana. This is counted as the beginning of the Achaemenid Empire, the Persian Empire. Cyrus went on to conquer Lydia in Anatolia and, in 539 BC, Babylon, and the empire became the largest the world had yet seen.

text.en: According to the Nabonidus Chronicle, a Babylonian source, the fighting against the Medes lasted at least three years, 553–550 BC. Cyrus had already become king in 559 BC, but was not yet independent. Both Wikipedia and Wikidata give 550 BC as the founding of the empire. The empire is also shown as an area on the map (Persian Empire).

summary.en: In the late 13th and early 12th centuries BC several societies in the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East collapsed. The Hittite Empire in Anatolia and the Levant fell, and the palace economy of Mycenaean Greece broke up into small, isolated villages. The New Kingdom of Egypt survived, but weakened. The trading city of Ugarit in Syria had been destroyed by 1178 BC. The source lists many possible causes, among them climate change, drought, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, disease and attacks by the so-called Sea Peoples. No explanation has won a consensus among scholars, and several causes probably worked together.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the collapse to the late 13th and early 12th centuries BC, and Wikidata gives 1200–1150 BC. Scholars disagree both about the causes and about how large the collapse was: recent research holds that it was more limited than previously thought, and that many of the destroyed cities have been misdated or lack evidence.

summary.en: A woman is buried in a seated position in a pit by Lake Oppmannasjön in north-eastern Scania, probably in spring. Radiocarbon dating places the skeleton between 7010 and 6540 BC, and it is one of the best-preserved skeletons from Sweden’s early Stone Age. She was found in 1939 and is now in the Swedish History Museum in Stockholm.

A pine paddle, almost 90 centimetres long, was found during peat cutting in 1927 or 1928 in the Åkermyra bog near Hedemora in Dalarna. Radiocarbon dating of the paddle in 2006 gave 7040–6640 BC, about the same time as the Barum Woman. The paddle shows that people could already build boats at that time.

text.en: The Swedish History Museum writes that the paddle was found in 1928 and is 87 centimetres long. The register of ancient monuments says it was found at Christmas 1927 and is 0.88 metres long. The date 7040–6640 BC rests on a single radiocarbon measurement from 2006; the museum’s object record gives a wider range, 9500–6800 BC.

summary.en: Around 5200–5000 BC, a person probably aged 25–30 is buried in a pit of sand coloured with red ochre at Manjärv in Norrbotten, then a small island off the coast. One or two more people are buried there later, and the grave is covered with a round stone packing. The red ochre graves of Norrbotten are the oldest known graves in Sweden with a stone structure above ground.

At Tybrind Vig on western Funen, Stone Age people of the Ertebølle culture live on the coast. The settlement now lies under water and was found in 1978. Because wood and other organic material survived there, dugout boats, decorated paddle blades, fishing gear and textiles have been found.

text.en: Lex dates the settlement to the Ertebølle culture, 5400–3900 BC. The Swedish History Museum places it in the late Mesolithic, roughly 5500–4000 BC. Lex’s dates are used here.

summary.en: Around 3900–3600 BC, people live at Lillberget, then an island in a coastal bay, hunting seals and fishing. They make Comb Ware, a pottery tradition also found in northern Norway, Finland, Russia and the Baltic region. Copper and amber from other areas, and flint from both southern Scandinavia and Russia, show contacts over long distances.

Around 3500–2800 BC, people in Falbygden in Västergötland build passage graves from large stone blocks. About two thirds of Sweden’s known passage graves lie there. The grave at Rössberga held the bones of 128–131 people, and DNA suggests that different family groups used different parts of the burial chamber.

From around 4200 to 500 BC, people carve images into the bedrock at Alta in Finnmark, the largest collection of rock carvings with hunting motifs in northern Europe. Reindeer, elk and bears are the most common, but there are also scenes of hunting, fishing from boats and rituals. The first carvings were found in 1973, and the site is a World Heritage Site.

text.en: Store norske leksikon and English Wikipedia date the carvings to 4200–500 BC from the shoreline of the time. According to English Wikipedia, the researcher Jan Magne Gjerde moved the oldest phases back by about 1,000 years in 2010.

summary.en: At Astuvansalmi in the Saimaa lake system, people paint images on a cliff by the water, roughly between 4000 and 2200 BC. The oldest paintings are the highest up, because the lake level was higher then. There are about 70 or more than 80 figures, depending on the source, including elk, people, boats and hands.

text.en: The Finnish Heritage Agency’s register of ancient monuments dates the figures to the time after the Vuoksi broke through, around 4000–2200 BC, and counts more than 80 figures. English Wikipedia dates the oldest paintings to around 3000–2500 BC and gives about 70 paintings.

summary.en: A young woman aged 16–18 is buried in an oak coffin in a burial mound at Egtved in Jutland, together with a child aged 5–6. The tree rings of the coffin show that the tree was felled in 1370 BC, and a flower in the coffin shows that it was summer. Her woollen clothing with a corded skirt is unusually well preserved.

In the 14th century BC, a bronze horse pulling a disc gilded on one side is made, all mounted on wheels. It is thought to show the idea that the sun was carried across the sky every day. The object was deliberately broken and placed in a bog on Zealand, where it was found during ploughing in 1902.

Around 1100–1000 BC, a seven-metre-high burial mound is built in the Håga valley near Uppsala, on a headland in a bay of Lake Mälaren. It is Scandinavia’s most gold-rich Bronze Age grave, with finds including a gold-decorated sword. Legend said that a Viking king lay there, but the excavation in 1902–03 showed that the grave is much older.

At Eskelhem vicarage on Gotland, two sets of horse gear are buried more than 2,500 years ago, probably as an offering to a deity. They included bits, jingling rings, a large openwork bronze disc and a belt bowl from a woman’s dress. The gear was made in Central Europe and is among the oldest in Sweden.

On a long ridge near Rauma in Finland, people build 33–36 burial cairns of granite boulders, from around 1500 to 500 BC. The youngest burial may date from the beginning of the Iron Age. The site is one of the largest and most complete Bronze Age sites in Fennoscandia and became a World Heritage Site in 1999.

text.en: English Wikipedia gives 33 cairns from 1500–500 BC. The Finnish Heritage Agency’s register of ancient monuments counts 36 cairns and says that the youngest burial was made only at the beginning of the Iron Age, so the site was still in use then. The register gives no calendar year for the end.

summary.en: A man aged 30–40 is hanged and laid in a bog near Silkeborg in Jutland, around 400 BC. He was found by peat cutters in 1950 and was so well preserved that he was first thought to be a recent murder victim. His face is the best preserved of all bog bodies.

text.en: Lex says the man was about 30 when he died. English Wikipedia gives 30–40 years and elsewhere about 40.

summary.en: About 7,700 years ago the Mount Mazama volcano in the Cascade Range, in what is now Oregon, had a huge eruption. Around 61 cubic kilometres of magma was thrown out, and ash fell over eight of today’s US states and three Canadian provinces. When the magma chamber beneath the mountain emptied, the summit collapsed into a large basin, a caldera, and the mountain became about 1,200 metres lower. The caldera filled with water and became Crater Lake, which at 592 metres is the deepest lake in the United States. Indigenous peoples have lived in the area for at least 10,000 years, and the volcano has an important place in their stories. In Klamath the mountain is called Tum-sum-ne.

text.en: Wikipedia gives about 7,700 years ago. A 2026 study of Yellowstone uses the ash from Mazama as a time marker and dates it to 7,584–7,682 years before 1950, based on a 2015 dating; this agrees with Wikipedia. Wikipedia writes that the USGS calls the eruption the largest explosive one in the Cascades in a million years, but that newer studies suggest an eruption at Lassen about 600,000 years ago may have been larger. That is why it is not called the largest here.

summary.en: The Budj Bim volcano in south-western Victoria, Australia, erupted about 36,900 years ago, plus or minus 3,100 years, according to an argon–argon dating from 2020. Lava and ash came out of a row of fissures and craters. A lava flow, the Tyrendarra flow, ran more than 30 kilometres south all the way into the sea and changed how water drained in the area, so that large wetlands formed. Much later the Gunditjmara people built their eel traps in them. The Gunditjmara creation story is about the eruption of the volcano, when the creator being Budj Bim was revealed. The name Budj Bim means “high head” in the Gunditjmara language.

text.en: Older datings gave only minimum ages, first 6,000–27,000 years and later at least 30,000 years. The 2020 dating gave 36,900 years, plus or minus 3,100 years with 95 per cent confidence. The nearby Tower Hill volcano was dated at the same time to about 36,800 years, plus or minus 3,800 years, and tools under the ash there show that people were in Victoria by then at the latest. That the eruption lives on in Gunditjmara oral stories is a possible interpretation raised by both Wikipedia and the 2026 study, not a firm conclusion. Both Wikipedia and the 2026 study rely on the same dating, Matchan et al. 2020, so they are not two independent datings of the eruption.

summary.en: In the Grotte des Pigeons cave at Taforalt in north-eastern Morocco, hunter-gatherers buried their dead about 15,100–14,000 years ago. At least 34 skeletons of adolescents and adults, and also of younger children, have been found, and the site is counted among the oldest burial grounds in North Africa. The same area was used for burials again and again, and some graves were covered with large stones. Some held horns, jaws and teeth from animals as well as plants such as ephedra, which may point to rituals. The people belonged to the Iberomaurusian culture. Cavities in their teeth and isotopes in the skeletons show that they ate a lot of plant food, such as acorns and pine nuts, several thousand years before farming reached the region.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 15,100–14,000 calendar years ago and calls the site possibly the oldest burial ground in North Africa. The 2024 study says the skeletons are directly dated to 15,077–13,892 years before 1950 and calls the site one of the oldest. That is why it says “one of the oldest” here. People used the cave much earlier, according to Wikipedia from about 85,000 years ago.

summary.en: At Skedemosse on Öland, then a lake that was becoming overgrown, people offer weapons, animals and gold over a long period, from the pre-Roman Iron Age to the late Viking Age. It is the largest find of weapon offerings in Sweden. Horse meat was eaten at ritual meals, and about thirty people were also sacrificed.

At the Sibudu rock shelter in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, stone points have been found with wear traces suggesting that they were mounted on arrows and shot with a bow about 64,000 years ago. A bone point, possibly an arrowhead, is about 61,000 years old. These would be the oldest known traces of the bow and arrow. Sibudu has also yielded one of the oldest known bone needles, about 61,000 years old, and glue made of plant gum and red ochre that was used to fix stone points to shafts. Sibudu became a World Heritage Site in 2024 together with other Stone Age sites in South Africa.

text.en: According to the source, the same wear traces form on the tips of spears, darts and arrows, and no test that tells thrown spears from arrows has been carried out. The researchers base the arrow interpretation on the context: the people hunted many different animals, including fast animals and animals that live in trees, which points to traps and snares and thus to cords that could also be used for bows. That is why it says here that the traces suggest bow and arrow, not that it is certain.

summary.en: In 1987 a Fulani herdsman digging a well near the village of Dufuna in north-eastern Nigeria struck a canoe 4.5 metres below ground. It is hollowed out of a single trunk of African mahogany, 8.4 metres long and 50 centimetres wide. Radiocarbon dates place it about 8,500–8,000 years ago, which makes it Africa’s oldest known boat and the second oldest in the world after the Pesse canoe in the Netherlands. The bow and stern are skilfully shaped, and the excavator Peter Breunig argued that this shows a long tradition of boat-building. The site probably lay on the flood plain of Lake Chad at the time, and the canoe was perhaps used for fishing.

text.en: The canoe has been radiocarbon-dated at least twice, and the two results do not overlap: 6556–6388 BC and 6164–6005 BC. The whole span is shown here. A charcoal sample from the site gave 8,500–8,000 years.

summary.en: A baboon fibula about 8 centimetres long, with a row of incised notches, was found in Border Cave in the Lebombo Mountains between South Africa and Eswatini. The bone has been radiocarbon-dated 24 times and is 43,000–42,000 years old. The notches differ in cross-section, so whoever carved them changed tool or edge. Peter Beaumont, who found the bone, believes the notches belonged to rituals. Others interpret the bone as a tally stick. No one knows for sure what the notches meant. The bone is far older than the Ishango bone, and the two are sometimes mixed up.

text.en: The bone has no coordinate of its own. The point on the globe is Border Cave, where it was found, with the coordinate from Wikidata.

summary.en: On the shore of an ancient lake in the Ténéré desert in Niger lies Gobero, the oldest known cemetery in the Sahara, from about 7500 BC. The Sahara was greener then, and the lake was about 3 kilometres across. The first inhabitants, the Kiffians, were hunters, fishers and gatherers who mostly stayed in the same place, and they buried their dead with the legs tightly drawn up against the body. When the climate turned dry, they left the site around 6200 BC. After a break another people, the Tenerians, arrived, who also kept cattle. About 200 graves have been found. In one of them a woman and two children lie facing each other with their hands intertwined.

text.en: The 2008 study is based on 78 radiocarbon dates and 9 OSL dates. It dates the first settlement to 7700–6200 BC and the oldest cemetery to about 7500 BC. Wikipedia relies on the same study but says “around 8000 BC” for the site in its introduction and 7550–6250 BC for the Kiffians. The span here is the first settlement.

summary.en: In the Apollo 11 rock shelter in south-western Namibia, seven grey-brown quartzite slabs bearing drawings were excavated. They are radiocarbon-dated to about 30,000 years ago and are regarded as the oldest pictures in Africa that depict something. On the best-known slab, animal and human are blended into a single being: the hind legs resemble a person’s, the horns and body an antelope’s and the head that of a big cat. People used the shelter in bouts over at least 40,000 years, from about 71,000 to 29,000 years ago. The archaeologist Wolfgang Erich Wendt named the cave after the Apollo 11 spaceflight, which had just returned to Earth.

At the Diepkloof rock shelter on the west coast of South Africa, about 270 pieces of ostrich eggshell with engraved geometric patterns have been found, from an estimated 25 containers. The shells were used as water containers. The patterns, among them a band of lines crossed by close hatching, are about 60,000 years old. They occur in several successive layers, so the tradition lasted for several thousand years. The researchers think the patterns may have expressed the identity of a group or a person. The engravings are among the earliest traces of people using symbols. Diepkloof became a World Heritage Site in 2024 together with other Stone Age sites in South Africa.

During the Ice Age large animals lived in Australia, among them the marsupial lion, giant kangaroos such as Procoptodon and the flightless bird Genyornis. Most of them died out. According to datings of fossils with OSL and uranium–thorium, all large animals on the mainland disappeared within a short time, about 46,000 years ago, roughly when the first people had arrived. A 2016 study of 659 fossil ages found that the extinction happened at roughly the same time for the different genera, with a peak about 42,100 years ago, and that it was not linked to drought in the climate. That study concludes that the megafauna disappeared about 13,500 years after people arrived. At Cuddie Springs in New South Wales stone tools have been found together with megafauna bones. The excavators see this as a secure association, but the interpretation is disputed.

text.en: The sources disagree on both when and why. Wikipedia gives about 46,000 years, the 2016 study a peak about 42,100 years ago (between 48,100 and 36,700 years for half of the dates). Another study found that 50 of 88 megafauna species have no dates younger than about 130,000 years, and some researchers think many species died out in stages before people arrived, because of the climate. The youngest known megafauna date is 33,000–37,000 years, for a Zygomaturus at the Willandra Lakes. The point on the globe is only an example; the animals lived across the whole continent. At Cuddie Springs, critics say the bones may come from older layers, and there are few cut marks on them.

summary.en: On Murujuga, the Burrup Peninsula and the islands off it in north-western Australia, there are around a million rock engravings, the largest collection in the world. They were made by chipping away the outer red-brown layer of iron oxide so that paler clay showed through. Many depict the thylacine, which is now extinct. Parts of the collection are estimated to be 40,000–50,000 years old, but how old the oldest engravings are is uncertain. There are also quarries, shell middens and campsites. The area belongs to the land of the Yaburara people and became a World Heritage Site in July 2025.

text.en: Wikipedia says that some engravings have been dated to more than 45,000 years and that parts of the collection are generally estimated at 40,000–50,000 years. A 2020 study is more cautious: the rock weathers so slowly that the art could have survived since people were in the area about 50,000 years ago. The span here shows the estimated age of the oldest engravings, not when all of them were made.

summary.en: During the Ice Age the sea stood much lower than today, and Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania were joined in one continent, Sahul. When the ice melted, the sea rose. The land bridge between Australia and New Guinea, the Arafura Plain, was flooded, and the Torres Strait formed. The sources give different times for this, about 12,000 or about 8,000 years ago. Between 8,000 and 6,000 years ago thousands of islands formed in the Torres Strait and along the coast of Australia. Many of the western islands in the strait are peaks of the old land bridge that were not submerged.

text.en: Wikipedia’s page on the Torres Strait Islands says the land bridge was most recently flooded at the end of the Ice Age, about 12,000 years ago. The pages on Sahul and on the prehistory of Australia say that New Guinea was separated from the mainland about 8,000 years ago, and the prehistory page that the islands in the strait formed 8,000–6,000 years ago. The span here covers all the figures. All three are Wikipedia pages.

summary.en: During the Ice Age Tasmania was joined to the Australian mainland by a broad land bridge, the Bassian Plain. People reached Tasmania across it about 40,000 years ago. When the Ice Age ended, the sea rose and flooded the plain. Bass Strait formed, and Tasmania became an island. The sources give different times for when this happened, from about 14,000 to about 6,000 years ago. After that the Tasmanians lived cut off from the mainland. People lived on Flinders Island in the strait until about 4,000 years ago.

text.en: Wikipedia’s page on Bass Strait says the strait formed about 8,000 years ago: the sea formed an embayment from 11,800 to 8,700 years ago, and about 8,000 years ago the rim was completely flooded. The page on Sahul says Tasmania was cut off about 6,000 years ago. The page on the prehistory of Australia says Tasmania was separated from the mainland about 14,000 years ago. The span here covers all three.

summary.en: Kilu Cave lies at the foot of a limestone cliff on Buka Island in Bougainville, Papua New Guinea. It is the oldest known settlement in the Solomon Islands archipelago, with traces of people from about 33,000–31,000 years ago. To get there, people must have travelled across open sea with no land in sight: from Nissan Island to Buka it is at least 60 kilometres. According to Wikipedia this is the oldest known evidence of such seafaring in the Palaeolithic. The people in the cave ate fish from both reefs and the open sea, sharks, sea snails, rats, bats and lizards. After a break at the end of the Ice Age, people lived in the cave again about 9,000–5,000 years ago.

text.en: The oldest radiocarbon date, on a sea-snail shell, is 28,740 ± 280 years BP. These are radiocarbon years, and Wikipedia itself converts them with a calibration curve to 31,560–29,850 BC, that is about 33,500–31,800 years ago. A 2022 review similarly gives about 33,100–31,400 calibrated years before present. The figures “about 30,000 years” and “29,000–20,000 years BP” on Wikipedia are uncalibrated. The span here follows the calibrated ages.

summary.en: Mount Gambier in South Australia is a complex of four maars, craters formed by explosive eruptions, among them Blue Lake / Warwar. It is one of Australia’s youngest volcanoes. According to the latest estimate, from radiocarbon dating of plant fibres in Blue Lake, the volcano erupted a little before 6,000 years ago. The Boandik people call the mountain Berrin. In their Dreaming story the lakes were ovens built by the creator being Craitbul, who is said to sleep at the bottom of Warwar.

text.en: Estimates of the volcano’s age have ranged from more than 28,000 years to less than 4,300 years. The latest estimate, a little before 6,000 years ago according to Wikipedia, is shown here. No independent second source has been compared.

summary.en: At the end of the Ice Age an ice dam blocked the Clark Fork River in what is now Montana, and a large glacial lake, Lake Missoula, formed. Again and again the ice dam burst, and the lake’s water rushed across what is now eastern Washington, northern Idaho and northern Oregon and down the Columbia River Gorge. Then the ice dam formed again. Researchers have found traces of at least 25 great floods, and the largest carried about 10 cubic kilometres of water an hour, 13 times more than the Amazon River. The floods carved out the Channeled Scablands landscape. The geologist J Harlen Bretz proposed the explanation in the 1920s, but it was disputed for 40 years.

text.en: Wikipedia says the floods came dozens of times during the 2,000 years between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago, on average about 55 years apart. A 2022 study says dozens of floods swept through between 18,000 and 15,500 years ago. The span here covers both. Older floods of the same kind happened during earlier ice ages, the oldest more than 1.5 million years ago.

summary.en: Lake Agassiz was a huge glacial lake in North America, fed by meltwater from the ice sheet. At its largest it was bigger than all the Great Lakes combined. About 8,200 years ago, when the last ice over Hudson Bay melted, the lake drained almost completely, probably together with Lake Ojibway, into the North Atlantic. This raised sea level across the world. The cold fresh water may have weakened the ocean currents in the Atlantic and caused the 8.2-kiloyear event, a rapid cooling that lasted two to four centuries. In Greenland the temperature fell by 3.3 degrees in less than 20 years. What remains of the lake includes Lake Winnipeg.

text.en: According to Wikipedia the cooling may have been caused by the draining of the glacial lakes, but it was probably only one of several causes: the outflow perhaps came on top of a longer cool period of up to 600 years. Estimates of how much the sea rose vary, from a few decimetres to a few metres. Wikipedia’s page on Lake Agassiz instead links the 8.2-kiloyear event, with the caveat that this is disputed, to a drainage 9,900–10,000 years ago.

summary.en: Lapa do Santo is a cave with a rock shelter in the limestone landscape around Lagoa Santa in eastern Brazil. The oldest graves there are about 10,600–10,300 years old, and the dead were then laid down whole. Around a thousand years later, about 9,600–9,400 years ago, things were done differently. The bodies of the dead were taken apart: teeth were pulled out, flesh was cut away, parts were passed through fire and perhaps some were eaten. Only after that were the remains buried, following fixed rules. There were neither grave goods nor large tombs; the rituals revolved around the bodies themselves. The people were hunter-gatherers who stayed in the same area and ate mostly plants and small to medium-sized mammals.

By the Sechin River in the Casma valley in Peru, about 330 kilometres north-west of Lima, lie the ruins of Sechin Bajo. In 2008 a German-Peruvian team found a sunken circular plaza there, 10–12 metres across, built of stone and rectangular mud bricks (adobe). Radiocarbon dated the plaza to about 3500 BC and a two-metre-high frieze nearby to about 3600 BC. If the dates are confirmed, they are the oldest known examples of monumental building in the Americas. People already lived in the valley around 4500 BC. The buildings were rebuilt several times, and the large buildings on top date from about 1600–1200 BC.

text.en: The source says the oldest dates need to be confirmed by further investigations. Calibrated radiocarbon dates of the first building range from 3700 to 2900 BC. The site competes with the Caral–Supe civilisation for being the oldest in the Americas; its oldest ruins at Huaricanga, 130 kilometres to the south, are dated to around 3500 BC.

summary.en: At Koster in the Illinois River valley in the USA, archaeologists have excavated 25 separate occupation layers, from the early Archaic period to about AD 1000. There are three dog burials that are about 9,900 years old. Together with a dog burial at Stilwell II, 35 kilometres away, they are the oldest known remains of dogs in the Americas. The site also has one of the oldest known cemeteries in eastern North America, and traces of people grinding food with stones and living in the same place all year round. The finds made archaeologists see the early inhabitants as settled rather than constantly on the move.

text.en: The source says the early Archaic period at Koster begins in “7500 BC”, but that the dog burials are 9,900 years old, that is about 7900 BC. The source does not explain the difference. The age of the dog burials is shown here.
